That the minister in charge of the act make a statement in the House advising why there has been a delay, whether or not a payment will be made under the act, and the date when it is expected cheques will be made.

Given the past dismal record of the administration of the Canadian Home Insulation Program, a few examples of which are perpetually late payments to home owners, shortage of application kits, lack of information, dishonest insulators fattening at public expense, and lackadaisical accounting practices which lead to home owners receiving double payments for the same job, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That this House urge the responsible minister to immediately tighten program procedures and controls so that Canadian taxpayers' money will not be squandered further.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter which should receive the unanimous consent of the House.
In view of the fact that the problems of inflation, unemployment and energy are global in nature, in view of the present international tensions that are a threat to world peace, and in view of this year's report of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, which includes 23 western industrialized nations, that Canada has the most decentralized government of all these nations, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Scarborough Centre (Mr. Kelly):
That this House acknowledge the need for a strong Canadian national government, and support the Prime Minister in the ongoing constitutional negotiations with the provincial premiers with regard to the split of federal-provincial powers.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
On April 17, I asked the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) to table the contract for the new fighter, the F-18, and cautioned him on the dangers in that contract. I further asked him about any contingency plans in the event of a United States decision to cancel the F-18 program. On May 6, the same minister was asked in the House by the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk (Mr. Bradley) to table the contract. On June 12, he finally tabled the contract without annexes, but promised in the House that he would make these annexes available to members of the House who requested them.
On June 20, I wrote to the minister to ask for the missing annexes to the contract which detail the financial commitments made on behalf of Canada, and since that date I have heard nothing. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson):
That this House directs the Minister of Supply and Services to table all the annexes to the fighter contract signed with McDonnell Douglas.

speechtext:

In view of the fact that Canada must move toward energy self-sufficiency, whereas the capacity of Canada to produce liquid portable fuels is declining, whereas the production of gasohol in Canada is technically possible on a large scale, and whereas many countries are now producing significant amounts of gasohol, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin):

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF FOREIGN INVESTMENTS BY FIRA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I am sure the minister is aware that since the last election 94 per cent of all applications to establish new businesses which went before the Foreign Investment Review Agency were approved, and that 85 per cent of all acquisition requests were approved, all this in spite of the fact the government has indicated that it wants to discourage foreign investment other than where it is of proven significant benefit to Canada.
Would the minister tell the House whether or not he has responded to the request in the letter written to him on June 12 by the United Electrical Workers Union asking for an investigation into the acquisition by Murata Manufacturing of Japan of Erie Technological Products of Trenton, Ontario, and whether or not he has looked into the subsequent lay-off of approximately 150 employees by Murata immediately after the acquisition took place and was approved?

speechtext:

(a)	October, 1977.

(d)	No.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
That this House deplores the Liberal government's indifference to the consequences of the global oil crisis and condemns its failure to provide a comprehensive energy program that would make Canada self-sufficient in energy.
She said: Madam Speaker, what the House is being asked to deal with today is a matter of urgency. Both the issue itself, that of international oil prices, and the increasingly limited, critical time frame that the government has to face up to this matter become more urgent with every passing day. Yet the government seems to be oblivious to the magnitude of the oil crisis, both in its international and in its domestic dimensions. Preoccupied as the government and its ministers have been

July 8, 1980
Energy
with a domestic pricing regime, it has failed to comprehend the threat that oil poses to the peace and security of the world and to international order as we know it. As a result, the Liberal government's inaction, its procrastination, its dithering, or call it what you will, daily compromises Canadian security, Canadian effectiveness in international organizations and Canadian flexibility in foreign policy.
Instead of showing its willingness to shoulder some of the responsibility to help rectify the situation, the government sends its ministers abroad to whine that Canada needs relief from an energy crisis not of its own making. But at the same time here at home ministers do Canadians the great disservice of trying to lull them into a false sense of complacency that no such global energy crisis exists.
Unfortunately several stark facts become daily more ominous. First, world oil production is not increasing, it remains static; if may even be decreasing. Second, world oil consumption and demand is going up, not down. Third, it is virtually impossible to switch overnight from the use of oil in such key sectors as transportation and heavy industry to the use of some new form of energy. It will take years of lead time to develop those alternative forms of energy and the technology to use them. Of course, in the meantime we will continue to be dependent on oil. Fourth, the struggle for these increasingly limited supplies of oil, even in the immediate future, will bring ever greater tensions between the eastern bloc and the western bloc, between underdeveloped nations and developed nations, and between suppliers and consumers.
These are stark facts, and all of these facts have been of increasing concern to thoughtful people in all countries of the world. But somehow or other that concern fails to penetrate the fog that substitutes for gray matter in the Liberal government. Indeed, it is only too true that they do not recognize the situation.
[ Translation]
The Liberal government did not even concern itself with Canada's vulnerability in this crisis. Seven months have passed since they cheerfully did away with the preceding government's energy policies which would have demonstrated Canada's will to come to grips with the international oil situation and the government has done nothing but waste seven crucial months.
I do not think this will have surprised us for the same group has obviously lost the better part of its time during the last seven years, or since 1973, when for the first time the OPEC countries made their power known.
The Liberal government has not in any way recognized the international oil situation. Nor does it have any understanding of the mounting tension from the implications the situation has on the security of our nation and on our foreign policy. [English]
There is no recognition by the Liberal government of the international oil situation, no understanding of the mounting tension it is producing globally, for the implications that has
for our nation's security or for the effect it has on the conduct of our foreign policy. There are no proposals to lessen Canada's vulnerability to the insecurity of offshore oil, no thought that Canada should be in the forefront of nations committed to face the reality of the situation and to take immediate steps, albeit difficult steps, to alter our present course. There is no recognition, no understanding, no proposals, no thought, and certainly no sense of urgency on the part of the government that there is an international oil crisis which cries out for action by governments of all countries.
It is for these reasons that today we have introduced a motion that deplores the Liberal government's indifference to the consequences of the global oil crisis and condemns its failure to provide a comprehensive energy program that would make Canada self-sufficient in energy. Virtually nothing is as vital to the stability of the western world as secure oil supplies. Yet nothing seems so far from reach. By their failure to blunt the initiatives of OPEC or to develop their own energy resources, Canada, the United States and other oil importing nations have left themselves vulnerable to oil-fired crises that could be havoc-wreaking. These include internal revolutions in the Middle East, conflict over oil supplies and financial ruin for many countries.
This gloomy scenario comes not from some doomsayer, but from Walter Levy, one of the best-known independent oil consultants. His thoughts are outlined in detail in the current issue of "Foreign Affairs". Nor is Mr. Levy alone in his harsh warning to oil dependent nations. There is a growing urgency among informed sources that the western industrialized nations have so far failed to "bite the bullet", failed to see the oil crisis for what it is and to take appropriate steps to reduce their dependency on offshore oil supplies.
The International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, England, recently commented as follows:
The west's most serious security challenge for the 1980s is how to assure the supply from an unstable third world of the raw materials on which its economic well-being, domestic stability and political cohesion has come to depend.
Those were words from the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
We all know that the most vital of the resources referred to is oil and that the most unstable area referred to is the Persian Gulf, which provides an essential part of the western world's oil supplies. In the world of today you cannot separate oil from security.
Recently the British secretary of energy warned of the dangers of regional and even global conflict as nations compete for oil resources. Last week in Moscow Chancellor Schmidt made the point that there could well be a worldwide struggle for the distribution of energy supplies. Indeed, the question of oil, its supply and security, has dominated world politics and international affairs since 1973. More and more, foreign policy objectives are inextricably linked to energy considerations.
This linkage was certainly made clear by former secretary of state Cyrus Vance at Harvard recently when he zeroed in on
July 8, 1980

the problems posed by declining domestic oil production on the one hand, and steadily growing imports on the other. Oil, he said, has the power to fuel inflation, undercut our trading position and determine the strength of our dollar. That is no mean feat for one commodity.
Vance warns that in meeting the energy crisis "we cannot rely on the genius of some economist with a new solution; we need acts of political will"; and he went on to predict:
If the United States and the other industrial countries do not act decisively to reduce our levels of energy consumption, and particularly our demand for oil, we will stand on the brink of economic disaster by the end of the decade-or sooner.
The International Institute for Strategic Studies in London warns of the security challenge oil poses; Mr. Vance warns of the economic disaster it threatens. The tragedy for Canada is that we have a government which lacks the political will to recognize and deal decisively with the energy crisis.

speechtext:
The first oil crisis, the one caused by the OPEC embargo in 1973, came as a shock to western economies. Long used to cheap oil-$1.37 per barrel was the average OPEC price only ten years ago-our economies became used to, and dependent upon, large quantities of imported cheap oil. For Canada, the First oil crisis seemed remote; after all, we were then a net oil exporter. However, between 1973 and 1979 Canadian oil production declined by almost 25 per cent, from approximately two million barrels a day to one and a half million, and it is still falling. In the same period, however, while our production was falling our consumption went up by some 200,000 barrels a day. As a result we have become increasingly dependent on offshore oil- offshore oil that is no longer $1.37 per barrel but ranges between $28 and $37 per barrel. But our energy policy, both domestically and internationally, has yet to adapt to this drastically changed situation.
Is it any wonder the 1979 "Annual Review" of the International Energy Agency warns that the maintenance of a continuing and possibly increasing gap between Canadian and international prices will create serious distortions in the Canadian economy? The IEA puts it this way:
If self-sufficiency is not attained and maintained, new public sector budgets will have to take into account permanent and possibly very expensive subsidies.
It goes on to state:
Demand will be greater than otherwise and supply less, and this will be reflected in the balance of payments position. In the medium to long run, it is questionable whether any country can successfully isolate itself on energy.
That is the comment of the International Energy Agency, and the implication obviously is that the Canadian government has for far too long played the short-term game of trying to
Energy
isolate itself from the reality of the world oil situation. This ostrich-like approach was evident in the comments of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) following his participation at the OECD meetings in Paris last month where much of the talk at that time was about energy. What did our Minister of Finance learn at those meetings? He learned there really is a crisis developing and that people outside Canada know about it. He said so in these words:
There seems to be a deeper consciousness in other countries than there is in Canada about the current world situation, and especially the impact of increased oil prices, and the possibilities of a slowdown worldwide.
Those were the words of our Minister of Finance. To think he had to go to Paris to learn that! To think he was so ill-informed he had not realized other western economies had long ago begun to take steps to reduce oil imports through conservation and consumer consciousness! To think he had not realized that the problem is not one of price alone but of supply and security of supply!
Even more serious, Mr. Speaker, is that the situation is likely to get worse, and it could become even more critical for any country which is dependent on offshore oil. There is a growing awareness that, for a variety of reasons, political, economic, financial and technical, OPEC production through the 1980s may be substantially lower than previous estimates have suggested, and the International Energy Agency forecasts serious shortfalls in production before the end of the decade. That agency now estimates that world production levels will not be higher through the 1980s than they were in 1979, and that is a change. These production levels will not be higher, so the very serious adjustment problems which were previously foreseen for the mid-to-late 1980s may well be with us now on a continuing basis and, what is even worse, in a climate of heightened political uncertainty.
The International Energy Agency reports that the anticipated global oil shortfall for 1985 appears likely to reach some three million barrels per day. By 1990, due in large part to declining availability of oil in the world market, the shortfall is expected to reach eight million barrels per day. I should add that these projections are based on the assumption that there will be no interruption of supply, either by further Iran-like revolutions or by oil producing countries deliberately turning down the tap. Yet just over the past weekend, the Iraqi oil minister, in a dramatic change of policy, joined Kuwait, Libya and Venezuela in calling for a limit on crude oil production among OPEC members.
The global shortfall of eight million barrels per day by the end of the decade is not the worst-case scenario, but rather one based on a comprehensive assessment of current realities- economic, political and strategic. Even if new resources were to come onstream, the lead time required to make them operational will take up most of this decade. So we are faced with a global shortfall of eight million barrels per day before we can even hope to bring on significant new sources of energy.

There are two additional frightening aspects to the present oil crisis. The first is the crushing burden oil imports place on the Third World, and the second is the danger to world stability as Soviet oil reserves begin to decline. With regard to the Third World, the International Monetary Fund calculates that this year alone OPEC will have a combined balance of payments surplus of some $115 billion, while the payments deficit of oil importing developing nations in the Third World will amount to $68 billion, an amount which these countries just cannot pay. The problems that these imbalances pose to the international financial system will be examined in greater detail by my colleague, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson).
There is also the question of the growing demand for oil by Third World countries. Some 90 of these countries presently consume four million barrels of oil a day. By 1990 it is estimated that their requirements will increase to 14 million barrels a day. So we have a situation where, at a time when the globe shortfall is expected to reach eight million barrels a day, these poorest of the poor countries will require an additional ten million barrels a day. Surely they will have the right to expect it and, indeed, they will demand it. The competition for scarce supply will be tough.
Second, and further complicating the picture, is the spectre of the Soviet Union going after oil supplies in the world market. The Soviet Union and its satellites are projected to shift from a net export position in 1979 to a net import position of at least one and possibly two million barrels per day in 1985, again at a time when a shortfall is predicted. Let us face it, Mr. Speaker: the Soviet Union will have to import oil and they cannot afford the large amounts of foreign exchange to buy that oil.
Analysing this situation, a U.S. intelligence report states that this-
-sets the stage for an East-West competition for mid-East oil, adding yet another potentially destabilizing ingredient to an area which already has experienced wrenching political events in the past year or so.
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan places the Soviet Union in an advantageous strategic position, both in relation to the oil-rich fields of the Persian Gulf as well as the important sea lane of the Strait of Hormuz, through which two thirds of the world's oil passes. Already through a blend of military buildups, subversion and diplomatic initiatives, the Russians appear to be manoeuvring the oil producers into a position where they would offer to pay for Arab oil by bartering commodities or military hardware instead of paying hard cash.
If that does not work, strategically they are in a position to seize the oil. Let us not be naive in our assessment of the potential of the Soviet Union to cause mischief through covert blackmail and subversion or, worse, through overt military action.
A further dimension to the vulnerability of the western countries because of their dependency on mid-East oil is the way in which it has begun to circumscribe their foreign policy. As the New York Times recently editorialized:
The cost of oil dependency cannot be measured only at the pump.
It is increasingly apparent in all aspects of foreign relations. We have seen that as new policies have been worked out between Saudi Arabia and the United States, and between Saudi Arabia and Denmark. It is as I have said: many countries will have to come to new foreign policies as the result of almost total dependency on mid-East oil and, in doing so, their foreign policy becomes hostage to their energy needs. However gloomy this is, it is the global reality.
We must ask ourselves: Where does Canada find itself as we enter this perilous decade? We find that our production of oil from conventional sources is down by 25 per cent in the past seven years, whereas our consumption of energy, and of oil in particular, is up last year alone by some 4 per cent. Knowing that our production was dropping and that our consumption of petroleum was rising, knowing that the previous Liberal government had doomed Canada to a course where it had to rely increasingly on imported, costly oil, the Clark government recognized that energy self-sufficiency was an objective we had to tackle with a sense of urgency. Indeed, the future of our country demanded no less.
As a government we saw the linkage between oil and security, between oil and foreign policy, and between oil and economic stability, so we undertook commitments in Tokyo which were designed to reduce Canada's dependency on offshore oil. We recognized the dangers of further exposure that offshore demands would create and present to this country. At Tokyo we undertook, along with our summit partners, to limit our imports of oil through to 1985. That meant two things. It meant that we had to reduce our growth of oil consumption to 1 per cent a year, and that we had to initiate a comprehensive energy program that would ensure self-sufficiency.
The tragedy for Canada is that the Liberal government has abandoned this policy and these commitments. Whereas we had committed Canada to limit oil imports to 600,000 barrels a day by 1985, it is projected that without the comprehensive program we proposed, Canadian imports will reach more than 800,000 barrels a day by 1985. Whereas we had undertaken to reduce the growth of oil consumption to 1 per cent a year, it is now reaching 4 per cent annually. Whereas we had presented to the Canadian public a comprehensive energy program designed to make Canada energy self-sufficient by 1990, the Liberal government has proposed nothing.
Canada, under Liberal leadership, has decided that rather than be part of the solution to this international oil crisis, it will put the country in the position of being part of the continuing problem. If you want some backup for that statement, Mr. Speaker, just read the OECD report released today which says that Canada has the second worst record among 17 developed countries in trying to conserve and find new sources of energy. But that is exactly what the Clark government's energy program was determined to correct.
Today, there is no longer the same sense of urgency that we attached to the development of oil sands and frontier sources, to the creation of alternate forms of energy, to the building of
July 8, 1980

pipelines where none now exist, to incentives for energy substitution and, most importantly, to greatly increased emphasis on the need for conservation. We as a government knew that Canada had the potential to become energy self-sufficient and we set about doing so.
Our target for self-sufficiency was 1990. That is also the year the International Energy Agency forecasts that there will be a global oil shortfall of eight million barrels per day. The Conservative government had committed itself to making sure that Canada was not hostage to that shortfall, not to the prices it would impose, not to the insecurity of supply it would subject us to, and certainly not to the manipulation of our foreign policy that it would invite.
The Liberal government, not having worried about these things for the previous seven years, not having felt the need to come to grips with the international oil crisis, not having considered it necessary to work out a comprehensive energy policy for Canada, is once more bent on trying to delude the Canadian people into believing that the oil question is some mere domestic squabble contrived for partisan purposes.
In so doing, the government limits Canada's flexibility and credibility in foreign policy. Just ask any of the countries that were at the Venice Summit. It makes us increasingly vulnerable to the global struggle for oil, and denies to us the independence we have a right to expect and which energy self-sufficiency could provide.

I disagree with that. I do not think we need more new foreign policies but we do need a new domestic policy. Will hon. members just listen for a moment. If we were to become self-sufficient, we could be isolated as much as it is possible to be from the harsh realities of the world today.
Energy
I have just finished reading a little paperback book which I am sure many other Canadians have read as well. It is called "The Seven Sisters" by Anthony Sampson. It outlines the history of oil and especially the history of the oil companies. I will read the last paragraph which is very relevant to our debate today. In a postscript written immediately after the crisis of 1979, Sampson had this to say:
But the problem of controlling the companies is only part of the broader question of national self-discipline and restraint. It is convenient for the western powers to use OPEC as their scapegoat, and to criticize the Middle Eastern nations for their reluctance to increase production. But the insatiable consumption of the west is putting those nations, particularly Saudi Arabia, in an impossible position with regard to their internal and external politics; and the only effective escape from a future oil crisis will not lie with increased Middle Eastern production, but with more serious western conservation and economies. The real lesson of the crisis can only be: we have met the enemy-it is us.
Today, I will focus on how we in Canada can become energy self-sufficient, and in that I think I am going to depart from the position of the other two parties.
I agree with the second part of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that the present Liberal government has failed to provide a comprehensive energy program. But what else is new? They have had years in office but they have not produced an energy program, and I doubt if they ever will. The minister has tried to come forward with a program but it is riddled with inconsistencies.
Our past record of resource regulation and development in Canada is unworthy of us as a people. There has been a vacuum in public policy. We should not blame it on the world situation but instead should look at the enemy, which is here.
In the recent past we were told that we were rich in unused energy and that our main problem lay in finding buyers for the surplus. Now we are being told that shortages are on the horizon and that unless we pay big for these wonderful megaprojects, they are not going to get off the ground and we are not going to have any oil. We appear to be doomed to a perpetual cycle of shortages and foreign ownership, not surpluses.
Canadian governments, it seems to me, think like foreign-controlled oil companies. We have allowed our future energy reserves-not the stuff we have been using and have been giving away, but the oil sands, the Mackenzie delta reserves, the High Arctic reserves, uranium and coal deposits-to be controlled by the same corporations that control our present conventional resources. We have sold out our oil and now the minister and his colleagues are about to sell our natural gas by prebuilding the Alaska pipeline.
We all remember industry's claim in 1972 which was echoed by the then minister, Hon. J. J. Greene, that Canada's oil reserves would keep the country in a state of self-sufficiency not for one year or a decade but for hundreds of years. What did we do then? We exported three billion barrels of oil. Then we were told that there was a shortage. Now we are being told there is a gas surplus and that we will have to export it. In a few years' time no doubt we will be told that there is a shortage. That is the kind of policy that has been followed.

Energy
We have a clear continentalist oil policy. The seeds were planted long before the fruit of the 1961 national oil policy appeared, whereby eastern Canada would consume Venezuelan oil and western Canada producers would look to United States markets for their surplus production. Today we have a shortage of oil and pay $3.7 billion into the compensation fund, mainly for the Atlantic provinces. Because of that and because of the uncertainty of the oil situation, the government cannot bring down a budget and 1 suspect-although he probably would not agree with me-that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is not going to get constitutional change without a settlement of the resource question, specifically an oil pricing policy.
We must have a new national energy policy and the basis of that policy must be to break away from the historic pattern of foreign control of Canadian resources. For the New Democratic Party this is the key to the problem. Unlike the other two parties we say that, to make Canada self-sufficient in oil and self-sufficient in energy, we have to break away from foreign control. We can be self-sufficient if we do that; that is the key. I hear my friend to the right asking me what our position is, and I tell him that I am outlining our position.
It appears that the position my Conservative friends are maintaining and articulating is that price is the key. That is what I pick up. I cannot figure out the Liberals; they are still in the muddled middle. The minister is still trying to squeeze by. I notice he is getting thin. He is going to be even thinner if he tries to squeeze by that Liberal energy promise to Ontario. If he could just get by this year, he might just narrow it down enough that it is not more than $4 a barrel for this year; then he can sock it to us next year. Yet I still say he is getting out of his promise to have a lower price than the Conservatives'. That is no energy policy at all. At least my friends to the right are prepared to articulate their policy.
I am saying that we have a third option or policy. We say that the Canadian people can move to self-sufficiency if a move is made to control the oil companies and the large energy companies in Canada. This will be a big challenge. Sometimes I look across the floor and see the minister and his colleagues from Quebec and admire the fight they made to get their rightful place in confederation. As a young English Canadian, I sometimes feel a little bored with my country, especially the English part because we do not have anything to fight for and we do nothing.

Today we have the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands coming forward with a motion endeavouring to condemn the government for its "failure to provide a comprehensive energy program". The first time was within the first month of this government coming to office, and

Energy
again today two months later. The first time it was put forward by the energy critic and today by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. I wish that the government of which these two able members were a part would have attached the same importance to the question of energy when they were in office.
If we are going to talk about failure, as this motion tries to do, the dismal failure of the former government in the field of energy should be what this motion refers to. If we look back at the main elements of the energy policy of the previous government, essentially it was socking it to the consumers in that famous budget that was defeated by Parliament and which raised such an outcry in the country.
Second, it was to try and dismantle, dilute, dissolve, and I do not know what other verb to invent when referring to the so-called energy policy of the previous government vis-a-vis Petro-Canada, the only major Canadian institution set up in the last few years in the field of energy which has proved to be of such great significance in the few years it was in operation.
The hon. member spent a lot of time talking about the international energy situation. The only contribution the previous government made to this very delicate international energy situation, and particularly to the protection of Canadian interests in that regard, was their famous proposal to move the Canadian embassy to Jerusalem. That had the effect of Canada being blacklisted by every Arab country. It put us in a very difficult situation vis-a-vis OPEC. This situation was something the new government had to work at repairing as soon as it took office. That is the type of background that the previous government left us and it is the context in which we took office.
The hon. member referred to the international energy situation. What she described is established by many publications and authorities, but I submit that it is nothing new; it has been with us for several years. If the hon. member has bothered reading even the government documents of 1974 and 1976, she would have found in those documents as well as the studies made public at the time, such as the major study published by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in 1976 entitled "Energy Future for Canadians", that all the facts she referred to today in terms of the international crisis were referred to in those documents and put forward for examination by Canadians by the previous Liberal government.
The member from the New Democratic Party stressed the importance of dealing with the matter in Canada. He pointed out a very important fact, the exceptional and very privileged situation in which Canada is.
[ Translation]
I am convinced Canadians are not unaware of the world energy crisis but I think they are truly aware of the particularly privileged situation in which Canada finds itself. If we have a crisis in Canada, it is not an energy crisis. Canadians know that, despite any speech the hon. member may make. Canadians know basically that Canada is extremely rich in terms of energy resources, that considering its population, Canada is
July 8, 1980

undoubtedly the most privileged country in the world in terms of energy resources.
Today and for years now, Canada has been in a position of being not a net importer of energy but an exporter of energy, year after year. We are still today, even in the area of petroleum products, that is if you include gas and oil, a net exporter of petroleum products, a very large exporter, and I am talking about several net billion dollars of exports of petroleum products. I am not talking of exports of electricity or coal which, according to all forecasts, are going to increase considerably in the coming decade.
So Canada actually finds itself in an extremely favoured situation, an extremely privileged situation, a situation that is the envy of all industrialized countries with which we are in competition. However, we are facing a problem with respect to oil. Our oil production is not sufficient to meet our needs and, at the present and for several years already, we have had to import a large part of our consumption. We are now importing about 25 per cent of our domestic consumption. That situation is, of course, not very favourable. It is not a situation that we are very pleased to see developing but it is not, on the other hand, an insoluble situation-it is a situation that Canada can indeed meet in the coming decade. There is no doubt that Canada has not only the human resources but also the financial and physical resources to achieve total energy self-sufficiency, including oil self-sufficiency during this decade.
In order to achieve this energy independence during this decade, since the government took office it has worked very hard to put back in shape the energy policy which the previous Conservative government spent so much time attempting to dismantle rather than developing an energy policy of its own. As the hon. member should have known, the previous Liberal government established a policy in 1974 and then in 1976 which is quite clear and which is a matter of record. It is an energy policy which has been the envy of the OECD countries and which has been referred to by many other countries as a policy which they would have liked to be in a position to follow. Unfortunately, they were not in a position to follow it, and for a very good reason. They did not have the privileged situation Canada had, that is, of being able to rely on vast resources in the field of energy, even though we have to import part of our petroleum requirements.
When the Tories were in office we had the problem that 25 per cent of our oil requirements were imported. The result of that was that the Tories tried to resolve the problem by tying Canadians to having to pay 85 per cent of international prices, whatever they were, on all Canadian domestic consumption, including the 75 per cent which was produced domestically. We rejected that Tory policy. The people of Canada rejected that policy, and rightly so. As soon as we were elected and could recall Parliament, we presented to Parliament on April 4
July 8, 1980

in the Speech from the Throne the basic elements of the energy policy we intend to follow.

1 am sorry. If I may be allowed, I might refer hon. members to the elements of that energy policy. The first element is that an energy policy is critical to the success of the country's economic policies, and therefore we cannot have an economic strategy or an energy policy which would ignore the impact of energy decisions upon inflation, unemployment, regional development and money transfers in this country. We could not have an energy policy which would be developed in some kind of vacuum whereby we would have in the end slower economic growth, more unemployed and much higher inflation than Canada needs to have. That is a basic element of our energy policy.
The second one is that the price of Canadian oil must be based upon Canadian conditions and circumstances and not upon the vagaries of a turbulent and unpredictable world market. The last Summit of seven heads of industrialized countries in Venice condemned the recent increases imposed by OPEC as being intolerable, unnecessary and excessive. We have decided that the prices which would be established in Canada for Canadian consumers would be based on Canadian costs and Canadian conditions and would not be tied to the cartel-type of pricing which OPEC decides.
We have also indicated clearly that the made-in-Canada price for oil we are proposing will result in a lower price to consumers than the one which had been proposed in the budget of the previous administration and which had been rejected by Parliament and by the people of this country.
We have indicated, in addition, that a petroleum auditing agency will be established to report on the financial situation of petroleum companies and to administer criteria relative to Canadian ownership objectives. We have also indicated that we must reduce our dependence on imported oil by promoting conservation and by stimulating the production of new domestic energy supplies. We have also indicated that conservation measures will be designed and promoted relative to transportation, home and industrial use. We have also indicated that steps will be taken to encourage consumers to switch from oil to natural gas or electricity for home heating, and other steps will be taken to encourage more rapid substitution from oil to other energy sources. Finally, we indicated in the Speech from the Throne that Petro-Canada will be maintained and expanded as an instrument of public policy.
A new Canada oil and gas act for all the territories and offshore properties under federal jurisdiction will provide for increased exploration activity. It will also be designed to promote Canadian ownership and Canadian objectives.
An alternative energy corporation will be created to stimulate the development of new and renewable energy resources to
Energy
replace oil, and Canadian companies and investors will be given opportunities to involve themselves more heavily in the energy field. The government has set the objective of a 50 per cent Canadian ownership target for the petroleum industry by 1990.
In the few short months we have been in office a number of decisions have been taken on each and every one of these subjects toward the implementation of these policy objectives, and I would like in the few minutes at my disposal to refer to some of them.
In the area of energy conservation I have already had the opportunity to sign three agreements. The first was with the minister of energy for Saskatchewan, then with the minister of energy for Manitoba and lastly with the commissioner of the Northwest Territories. These agreements deal with energy conservation and renewable energy technologies. In these three agreements we have agreed to spend several tens of millions of dollars among ourselves to promote energy conservation and new renewable energy technologies in the various provinces.
There has been a conference between the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), on behalf of the federal government, and industry on energy conservation. That conference covered about 80 per cent of industry energy use, and at that conference there were reports from 15 different task forces set up by different sectors in response to a call issued to industry by one of my predecessors, the Hon. Alastair Gillespie. Fifteen different task forces have been set up, and they reported on the first five-year program which had been set up. We were pleased to see that industry had not only met its target of energy conservation, but had overtaken that target substantially. We got industry to commit itself to another five-year program of additional energy conservation. In this respect we have done as well as, and I would say even better than, any other OECD country in terms of co-operation with industry.
We have also extended during the past several months the Canadian home insulation program which probably has been the most important and successful of all conservation initiatives; and at present we are continuing research and preparation for a retrofit oil furnace program to improve the efficiency of home heating units. We are designing automobile mileage standards at present, and that measure will soon be brought forward before the House. The alternate energy corporation has been announced and a budget of $20 million has been set aside in Petro-Canada to cover the initial cost of that corporation. At present we are interviewing candidates to run that corporation, which we intend to set up in the near future.
While I am speaking about Petro-Canada I might also mention that one of the first things we have done since we have been in office has been to reassure the Canadian public that this government stood fully behind Petro-Canada. We intend to make PetroCan an even more significant instrument of energy policy in this country. As soon as we took office, we reinstated to the budget of Petro-Canada the $80 million

July 8, 1980
Energy
which the Conservatives had cut from that corporation when they were in office.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Petro-Canada has been very active ever since it has been shown that it has the support and confidence of the government. It announced in the last few weeks a project for a fourth tar sands plant with Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company, a project which could cost as much as $10 billion. This is the first totally Canadian-owned project in the tar sands area. This has been done thanks to the initiatives of Petro-Canada in co-operation with the Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company.
Petro-Canada also announced during the course of June three drilling programs in the Labrador Sea, and it is now the operator for a number of other companies in that frontier area which has a high discovery rate as compared to other frontier regions.
I should like to say a word now on oil and gas pricing; some of my colleagues have referred to it. I have indicated what our target is-a made-in-Canada price which will give all Canadians one uniform price at a level well below international levels.
In March I also indicated that, in order to achieve this target, I had the intention of invoking the force majeure clause in the tar sands projects, particularly the Syncrude oil sands project, in order to arrive at a cost to Canadian consumers for that oil, which will make it more and more important to arrive at a price which reflects the real economic cost of developing incremental oil supplies.
While discussing this matter with the government of Alberta, I indicated that we are continuing to pay compensation payments, subsidies which were provided under the previous agreements to the level of international prices. However, one area, which is probably even more important than the question of pricing itself in relation to the problem raised by this motion, which is security of supply, is the whole question of conservation. Because if there was one problem with the previous Conservative policy, it was its almost exclusive reliance on price as an instrument of policy in this field. It was what I would have called the baseball bat approach to energy policy: hit the consumer hard enough that he will not be able to afford the oil he needs.
In effect, there are many other ways of dealing with the problem. One has to do with conservation; the other has to do with substitution. I have already announced in the first few months since we have been in office a number of decisions by this government in order to move people to switch their consumption of energy from oil to other forms. In May I announced the government's policy and the government's goal to reduce the residential, industrial and commercial use of oil in this country to 10 per cent of their net energy requirements. The policies that we have under way and the others that we will announce shortly will permit attainment of this objective in most oil consuming sectors and areas within a decade.
Let me point out that to reduce oil use to 10 per cent would save about 150,000 barrels of oil a day in the residential field alone, another 150,000 in the industrial sector, and 75,000 in the commercial area, for a total saving of about 375,000 barrels a day in this country. At present the oil share of consumption in those fields is about 32 per cent. I am convinced that we can, without any harm to our Canadian consumers and Canadian industry, reach that 10 per cent level within the decade.
We also indicated in the Speech from the Throne that we were favouring the earliest possible construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritimes.

During the weeks which preceded today's motion, I had already had the opportunity to announce the decision of the government to approve the recommendation made by the National Energy Board to support the development and approve the immediate construction of a gas pipeline to serve the entire province of Quebec. The first section of this pipeline will go as far as Quebec City, and various branches will then supply the entire province so that the citizens of Quebec will be able to use natural gas rather than heating oil, which is much more expensive.

We have also indicated that the extension of that pipeline to the maritimes remained the preferred option of the present government, and we have been in touch with the sponsors of this project to review the reservations that have been expressed by the National Energy Board and to see what further steps are required to ensure that the maritime provinces will have sufficient gas available to meet their needs, whether that gas comes from the west or whether it comes from new discoveries in and around Sable Island.
Those measures of substitution which have been already announced are only some among others and I should like to mention another one which is of great significance. It has to do with making much better use of residual fuel oil in this country. During the month of May I announced that I have reached an agreement with the five refining companies to instal upgrading facilities in their plants which would provide a capacity to make better use of about 125,000 barrels a day of residual fuel oil. This will not only lead to the production of premium fuel, such as gasoline or heating oil, instead of unwanted and surplus heavy fuel oil, but it will also make way for natural gas and provide for a more efficient use of our total domestic and foreign petroleum supply. The net result again will be a reduction in our dependence on oil imports.
In terms of volume, these measures are the equivalent of the net addition to our oil supply which would be made by a $68 billion tar sands plant, and yet through the set of investments in the refineries which I have announced, Canada is getting this kind of production at half the cost and about three years sooner than it would come from a tar sands plant. I do not think there is a more telling rebuttal to the argument that only
July 8, 1980

through a pricing mechanism can we increase our total oil supply.
In the field of international energy, Canada has not been dragging its feet. In the last few months since we have been in office, I have had the opportunity of attending the ministerial meeting of the governing board of the International Energy Agency in Paris, of attending the Venice Summit and of meeting several times with my colleagues, the secretary of energy for the United States, the Australian minister for national development and energy and the Japanese minister of energy. We had the privilege of the visit of the Saudi Arabian energy minister, and I had the privilege of meeting with the minister of energy for Algeria, who at the present time happens to be the president of OPEC.
These meetings and discussions which have taken place with the representatives of those various countries achieved good results for Canada. Certainly as far as OPEC and the Arab countries are concerned, I think they have helped in re-establishing the normal relationships which existed and should have continued to exist between our respective countries but unfortunately had been seriously damaged by the foolish steps in the field of foreign policy of the previous Conservative government.
I should like to summarize the various initiatives taken by the government during the past four months under three broad objectives. The first is to achieve energy independence, which we believe can be done during this decade. As 1 have noted, this goal is being achieved by conservation measures particularly directed toward oil. Also 1 have cited measures to substitute other forms of energy for oil. There are major incentives for enhancing energy supplies, and we will be going further in this direction when the oil pricing negotiations and revenue sharing questions are settled. We continue to have strong research and development activity in this country, particularly directed to our unique conditions of climate, terrain and location.
Also I have spoken of the government's oil pricing policy, and closely associated with this is the objective of ensuring a distribution of benefits from oil and gas revenues to all Canadians. As I noted before, we want a revenue system so structured that as prices rise the national government will get the share it needs to carry out its national responsibilities. We need to have a national government which will have not only the powers but the resources to ensure that regional disparities in the country are not going to become excessive.
Also our pricing policy very much reflects the right of producing provinces and corporations to a fair return for their resources and their investment, as noted in the Speech from the Throne.
The Speech from the Throne placed considerable emphasis on the specific goal of at least 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry by 1990. The objective is to enable Canadians to participate in their energy industries.
Energy
The central issue in the matter of a Canadian energy program is how the costs and benefits of developing and using energy are shared among Canadians. The government's objective in each one of the projects I have outlined today-and there are many more-is to ensure a fairness in the complex process of harnessing energy supplies.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank my colleague for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) for giving us the opportunity to make very important comments on the energy situation. I would also like to say once again that 1 support the proposals that we have already made. I am quite certain that time will prove these proposals to have been quite reasonable.
At the same time I was rather surprised to hear the minister repeat his energy policy. Of course, he was referring to the throne speech which contains proposals which I believe we heard as far back as seven or eight years ago. When the minister said today unhesitatingly that there was no energy crisis, I believe he should have said that there is no hydroelectric crisis because we indeed have a surplus of this type of energy.
However, by making a simple calculation, we can see that this government has been in power 14 years and five months during the last 15 years. So I do not think that we can be blamed any longer for that lack of energy policy and that lack of foresight. In the circumstances, 1 think that talking as he did today the minister has demonstrated to all Canadians his incredible failure, the failure of his government to provide any measure, to have any foresight and to give any guarantee to Canadians when he confirmed, with regret of course, that we are still importing 25 per cent of our domestic consumption. He deplores it, of course, but what has been done during all these years? Today he comes with the same proposals that we have already heard, and that have not been implemented for political reasons. I remember very well that within a few months we had to take strong measures because of the inaction of a government which did not take the present situation seriously.
And the minister responsible does not hesitate to accuse the former government of having attempted to mislead the consumers because, Mr. Speaker, we had proposed measures which took reality into account, and which required courage, to put Canada back on the road to prosperity and reach all the objectives mentioned today by the minister, self-sufficiency and, of course, benefits for Canadians. Did we have to pay because of the failure of the previous government to do its job and take its responsibilities?
We had to present a budget and I think that we were trying to shoulder our responsibilities. We were not taxing those who are not using gas and this was important. I look forward to the next budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is still not able today to assure us that he rejects the idea of deindexation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the least we can say about the dubious situation in which the government finds itself is that it is the result of a Liberal and New Democratic conspiracy-we should not forget-to have Canadians believe that they could avoid higher oil prices more in line with international prices. I do not think there is anything new in this respect. How could anyone believe that the Liberals were sincere when for three or four years, if not six, they themselves had warned Canadians that the current oil subsidization program could not last forever and that sooner or later consumers in this country would have to pay for their oil at prices comparable to those of European, Japanese or American consumers?
Even the New Democrats, playing it both ways, had admitted the necessity of a price increase but they let Canadians believe that through some sort of miracle they could elude the fate of citizens of other industrialized countries in the free world. The New Democrats paid a stiff price for their complicity with the Liberals, Mr. Speaker, for not only were they frustrated in their own attempts at substantial electoral gains in Ontario, but they also favoured the re-election of the Prime Minister whose defeat they pretended to engineer. The New Democrats repeated their stupid tactic. In 1972, rather than give the Progressive Conservatives a true chance to show their stuff and find solutions to the practically insoluble problems they had inherited, the New Democrats sealed their pact with the Liberals. They simply put back at the helm the very people they pretend to attack publicly but whom they go on supporting and helping underhandedly.
Today the New Democrats are shocked that the Liberals are not keeping their more recent electoral promises, particularly with respect to oil, but could they give just one example of a situation in which the Liberals did not cheat the people, play on words, invent simplistic slogans, give out complicated formulas that no one understands or has any way of corroborating? Is the Liberal approach to the oil price issue not confirmation of their double dealing? The famous Canadian formula is but a lure which they used to regain power but already there are a number of indications which lead us to believe that in the long run the price Canadians will eventually have to pay for their oil will be the same as, if not higher, than the one foreseen in the budget submitted by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and this in the wake of I do not know how many denials, including the solemn promise made by the Prime Minister at the Bonn conference to spare no effort to see that Canadian oil prices would rise to international level. And all this while shelving the understanding between the Clark government and the Lougheed government, and doing nothing to avoid a new political crisis that might mean the end of Canada itself.
Indeed, the silence of the Prime Minister during the campaign should have alerted Canadian consumers to the sell-out being prepared. The Prime Minister and the Minister of
July 8, 1980

Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) were careful at that time not to give details of the famous made-in-Canada price they wanted to establish for oil. They were careful not to suggest that one of the means they intended to use was quite simply a probable infringement upon the constitution, laying their hands on Alberta's, Saskatchewan's and British Columbia's oil and gas resources.
What guarantees have we that, if the Liberals succeed in overcoming these three provinces, they will not tomorrow launch an attack on Quebec's hydraulic resources, and later undermine Ontario's industrial and mining potential, for the benefit of the central government? These are questions we should ask ourselves now. The proof is that in respect of Atlantic provinces, they want to shelve the generous Progressive Conservative policy and to recoup for Ottawa's sole benefit the control over offshore mining resources. The Liberal conspiracy to lure Canadians takes various forms, Mr. Speaker. In general, they avoid resorting to outright lies that would be too gross to be believed. Most of the time, they are content with half-truths, or if you will half-lies, subtle understatements or again, quite simply, mute silences.
The Liberals have a very particular propensity for the tactics of silence. That keeps them from having to give their constituents explanations which could put them in a disadvantageous situation. Indeed the example comes from the high circles. Did the right hon. Prime Minister himself not hide from Canadians, when he was asking them for his first mandate in 1968, that his true objective was to centralize federal powers even more in Ottawa? As everyone can see, bad habits are not easily lost. Not only have the Liberals misled the Canadian people by luring them with the possibility of freeing the country from international constraints in oil prices, but they have to be held directly responsible for the instability of our own energy supply sources. They have always ridiculed, verbally and in their policies, the energy self-reliance objectives which the Progressive Conservatives have been advocating for quite a long time. They have allowed the situation to get so bad as to force us to pay high prices to foreign suppliers while the present government refuses to Canadian producers the price it pays to foreign sources without raising an eyebrow.
Nobody is blaming the government for having created in 1974 a subsidy system to help Canadian consumers adjust to the price increases which were dictated by OPEC. But what should have been a temporary policy became a permanent policy. The most direct result of that lack of foresight and courage of the government is that Canadians continued to delude themselves, thinking that they could inconsiderately waste oil and pay indefinitely a price which is below the international level. Another result, Mr. Speaker, is the incommensurable increase in our balance of payments deficit and the ensuing pressures on the Canadian dollar. Finally, we should realize that if the price of Canadian oil had reached the international level as early as 1975 or 1976, billions of dollars
Energy
could have been invested in exploration for new hydrocarbon sources and new renewable energy sources. In order to gain electoral benefits in the short term, the Liberal party will have contributed to weaken the Canadian economy, to deceive consumers on the necessity of a sharp rise in the price of oil and at the same time it will have aggravated tragically our dependence on foreign energy sources for our supplies.
Further betrayal of the oil consumers by the Prime Minister and his government: did we not hear him, during the last election campaign, praise the merits of Petro-Canada of which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources spoke just a while ago? Did we not hear him say to whomever wished to listen to him that Petro-Canada would become the cornerstone of the policy on exploration and development of new sources of energy in Canada? What happened? In a reply to the leader of the NDP, a shortage of funds was invoked recently as the reason for dropping the presumably grandiose projects he had claimed to be planning with that Crown company. Is it any wonder the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) accused him of betrayal, but is the latter himself to be taken seriously? We heard from the very mouth of the right hon. Prime Minister-even while the NDP and especially its leader were castigating the Liberal party and its leader-that in the back rooms of their respective parties, they were discussing the possibility of a coalition government to stem the tide of Progressive Conservative popularity with the public. What confidence can we have in those two seemingly opposed political groups which down deep have but one objective, the subjugation of the citizens to the will and dictates of a state grown ever-present and all powerful?
But most obvious of all, despite appearances, the oil policy advocated by the Liberals and widely supported by the NDP benefits the rich unduly to the detriment of the working classes. A big fuss was made over the 18-cent a gallon of gas tax proposed by the Crosbie budget, but the Liberals and NDP carefully avoided telling the people that the same budget also provided, for the less well off and public transport companies, tax advantages that would have cushioned the effects of the price increases which were also designed to moderate consumption. What the Liberals and NDP failed to say to the consumers is that the present subsidy system is largely of greater benefit to the big than to the small oil consumer. At the present time, all Canadian taxpayers are called upon to pay, through their taxes and the money the federal treasury borrows, a subsidy of at least $20, if not more, for each barrel of oil imported from abroad.
Now, who benefits most from this subsidy? Naturally, those who consume more oil. And who are these people? The owners of castles like the one the right hon. Prime Minister bought for himself some months ago in Montreal. Whereas the average expense in heating oil for a modest bungalow is between $400 and $600 a year, that of the bourgeois palaces easily reaches $2,000 and even $3,000. One can easily conclude that the

Energy
bigger the house, the higher the heating costs and also the subsidy one gets from the state. The Liberal policy claims to help the poor but in reality it helps the rich take advantage of the largesse of a government seeking to protect their privileges.
To the heating costs of these immense castles, add the heating costs of the swimming pool with which they are practically all appointed; add the gas expenses for members of the family driving either big cars, sports cars, not to mention snowmobiles, yachts, or even motorcycles or Jeeps to get to the ski slopes or the resort areas. Add up these gallons of fuel burned by the people and you will realize that the true beneficiaries of this subsidization policy are not the poor people, Mr. Speaker, like members opposite would have us believe.
In fact, those who benefit are the richest elements of our society, playboys who can afford the luxurious homes, the latest cars, the expensive snow blowers, motorboats and what have you; those who can afford to spend the warm evenings dining in a high-class restaurant, attend summer theatre productions or simply while away the hours in the fresh air while the poor people, forced to pay part of the gas expenses, must be satisfied with sweating it out on their poorly ventilated balconies.
It is with a view to correcting this injustice that the Crosbie budget forced consumers to pay the true price for oil and provided tax relief measures to help the less fortunate. Mr. Speaker, it is against this act of justice that the Liberals and the New Democrats voted not too long ago. History will show that it is the Progressive Conservative Party which defended the true interest of the Canadian consumer. 1 have nothing against those who can afford the luxury of large houses and gas guzzling cars, absolutely nothing, but I cannot bear to see the poor being forced to pay part of the costs through their taxes. I do want richer people to enjoy their wealth but provided they do not waste a resource that is getting scarcer and scarcer and provided they pay an appropriate price for the fuel they use.
1 am not kidding myself, however, about the effect of my remarks on Liberal members opposite. Until the people decide to get rid of them and send them back in the opposition, we will witness the same little game of compromises and expedients, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, did the right hon. Prime Minister not warn us in 1963 that no burst of energy or burst of dignity was to be expected from the Liberals? In spite of his NDP past, did he not rather choose in 1965 to join the Liberal ranks because he knew that tool was malleable at will to implement his policies? The present Prime Minister knew, as he indeed wrote, one would not find in any other party the abject submission of members to the will and whims of its leader.
Did the recent Winnipeg convention not give us once again the example of a party incapable of thinking by itself, of giving itself policies that correspond objectively to the needs of this country? That convention gave us the proof once again that
July 8, 1980
that political formation no longer has any will of its own, but what counts for it to stay in power is to obey the leader even though its members know he is leading the party and the country to ruin.
It was a great pleasure to participate in this debate because I think Canadians must be reminded of the proposals we made. I think Canadians must also grasp the repeated promises of a government that has been in power for years and is trying once again to fool the people by repeating promises that have already been made. But we must remind Canadians-and it is our obligation to do so-that this government refused to take responsibilities that were necessary for the good operation of a country if one really wants to put this country back on the road to prosperity, and the government across has been doing the opposite up till now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) in this debate and listening to the empty rhetoric of his intervention, which was really in essence a pile of words supported by very few facts- and, if any, by the realization, which he unfortunately did not imply in his words, that he was re-elected by the slimmest majority that he has ever had since he entered politics-one is forced to look at the proposition before us today and to read it very carefully.
The Progressive Conservative party has put before us a motion which hinges on two words, "indifference" and "failure". Those are the two key words with which they would like to identify the Liberal government's energy and oil policy. July 8, 1980

A number of declarations were made by the opposition. They used phrases such as "government lacks the political will" and other sentences of which I made note. They offered no proposals on how to make Canada self-sufficient in energy.
There was nothing new on this subject in the speech of the hon. member from Kingston and the Islands or that of the member who spoke for the New Democratic Party. They had nothing to add to what has been said since the energy crisis in the world began. They gave us a regurgitation of ideas that have become commonplace. Nothing new has emerged today. In order to make their points the NDP quotes from books. That is the only way they can get their philosophy across in this House. They go back to 1920 and authors of the past in order to suggest what we should be doing in the present or the future. But they just come up with the same old chestnut about buying the industry. Of course, they do not tell the Canadian people what it would cost or where the money would come from and, if it were to come from increased taxes, how they would be increased and by how much. That is the extent of the NDP intervention so far today on this very central issue which is a puzzle to every nation in the world.
On the questions of how to reduce our dependence and how to become self-sufficient, the NDP repeated the old refrain of more renewables. Having said that, did they go on to tell us what share of the total energy package renewables, non-renewables, and so on, combined, would take care of? Are they able to tell us what the renewable energy sources can provide for the next five, ten or twenty years as an alternative to dependence on non-renewables today?
Judging from their performance so far, one can only wonder what contribution the official opposition can make by basing a motion on a charge of indifference and failure in light of the record of the Liberal party and in light of their own record. Only five years ago in this House they opposed tooth and nail, at every stage, the creation of Petro-Canada. It is incumbent upon those of us who believe that Petro-Canada has a central, vital role to play in Canada-where over the years we have developed a quite unusual balance between the public and private sector-to put on record some facts concerning Petro-
Canada. I shall be glad to devote a few minutes of the time that I have left to doing just that.
As my remarks have clearly indicated, Mr. Speaker, on February 22 Canadians rejected a government which had committed itself to privatizing Petro-Canada-the Progressive Conservative party. A decisive mandate was given to the Liberal party which had declared its determination to maintain and strengthen Petro-Canada as a fine instrument of public policy-a policy which is in the interests of the public sector.
Petro-Canada was under fire from the Progressive Conservative government but certainly not from the Canadian public. In fact, the process went so far that one Montreal newspaper characterized it as "the slow destruction of Petro-Canada". Happily, the situation has been reversed and Petro-Canada is again a dominant force in the development of our oil and gas industries. As well, it is functioning as the necessary intermediary in state-to-state arrangements which are taking shape to supplement, but not supplant, private oil import supplies.
As hon. members know, Petro-Canada has played and is playing a most important role in frontier areas of Canada. Apart from the Beaufort Sea, where the continuing efforts of Dome and its partners claim our attention, Petro-Canada is actively represented almost everywhere.
On the Labrador shelf, Petro-Canada is the operator for a group of companies which are maintaining a high level of exploration effort with three drilling units operating during the short season. Indeed, one of these units was recommissioned at St. John's just last Friday. This part of Petro-Canada's exploration program will involve the completion and testing of two important wells which were started last year, as well as the drilling of new wildcats.
The most promising success of the 1979 frontier exploration program was the Hibernia oil discovery on the eastern Grand Bank. Here Petro-Canada has a 25 per cent working interest in what is almost certainly our first major commercial oil discovery in the frontier areas. Three drilling units are presently operating in this area to facilitate continuous evaluation of these important prospects. Simultaneously, environmental studies are in hand to determine how development can take place with a minimum risk of environmental damage.
Another important success with which Petro-Canada has been associated is the Venture gas discovery off Sable Island, in which Petro-Canada has earned an approximately 30 per cent interest. This discovery is the first potentially commercial gas discovery to be made in the eastern frontier area. It is obviously strategically located in relation to supply for the energy deficient Atlantic provinces.
In the north, Mr. Speaker, Petro-Canada has a 48 per cent interest in Panarctic Oils Limited. Successes there have included the major Whitefish gas discovery, estimated to contain as much as one trillion cubic feet of natural gas. In 1980 and 1981, Petro-Canada will finance over 80 per cent of

This high level of Petro-Canada participation results from a lack of budgetary commitment from the private sector partners of Panarctic to continue funding their representative shares. That in itself commands the attention of the Progressive Conservative Party to the presence of a publicly-owned Crown corporation, such as Petro-Canada.
