speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have heard today from the other side on this very important motion which my friend, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), has put forward today is an illustration of the total lack of understanding that is quite clearly seen in the government benches. I have been waiting to hear whether there is any understanding of the serious nature of the international issue that we are facing. All that we have had is a repeat of the halfway attempts which the government and the previous Liberal administration have made in trying to come to grips with this problem. But as my hon. friend has said, there has been a total lack of understanding and an inability to come to grips with the political necessities and the very tough political decisions that are essential here if we are to avoid the exposure we are facing today.
I would like to commence my contribution to this debate on the serious state of Canada's energy policy in this increasingly unstable world by quoting what Cyrus Vance, the former U.S. secretary of state, said:
In meeting the energy crisis ... we cannot rely on the genius of some economists with a new solution. We need acts of political will.
This is what is lacking in this government and in previous Liberal administrations since 1973 when this problem first arose.
The challenge and the clear feasibility of achieving energy self-sufficiency has been before us for many years. The pressing need for action has been clear. The opportunity for massive economic development is equally clear, and still the govern-
Energy
ment has not accepted energy self-sufficiency as a clear policy objective.
The first time action was taken and the first time the opportunity was recognized and acted upon was by the Clark government last fall. Sadly for Canada, this far-sighted initiative was defeated by the near-sighted political opportunism of the Liberal-NDP coalition last December.
The tragedy and frustration of this government's inactivity on the energy front is best illustrated by the recent Venice Summit. In paragraph 7 of the communique, the seven leaders said it all, as follows:
To this end, maximum reliance should be placed on the price mechanism and domestic prices for oil should take into account representative world prices. Market forces should be supplemented where appropriate by effective fiscal incentives and administrative measures. Energy investment will contribute substantially to economic growth and development.
This could have been the preamble to the Clark government's comprehensive energy policy announced last fall. But what did the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) do? It is difficult to understand how he can defend his so-called energy policy to his Summit colleagues. Instead he appeared to walk away from the meeting and laugh in the faces of the other six leaders. With this much respect for commitments by world leaders on such an important matter, it is a wonder that the Prime Minister bothers to attend these meetings.
The Prime Minister said that Canada should not be servilely bound to world oil prices which the Summit nations then violently condemn. These are soothing words for the folks back home, but this rhetoric has nothing to do with the energy reality of today.
How can we have his so-called made-in-Canada energy price when oil imports could reach as high as 45 per cent of our oil consumption by the mid-1980s? That is the most critical element of Canada's energy position, and that is the element around which we have to build an energy policy. This is the key problem. With no change in energy policy, we will continue to pay more and more money for more and more foreign oil in an increasingly volatile international environment.
During the recent election campaign I spoke frequently of "security of supply". I wish to elaborate on some aspects of this security, or shall I say "insecurity", for this government's inaction has exposed this country in two important areas to greater worldwide instability than we have ever seen. The tragedy of it is that it has been and is still within our power to reduce this exposure. We are now greatly exposed to the increasingly volatile international scene through the greatly increased cost of oil imports and through our chronic balance of payments deficit.
Let me set out the magnitude of this problem. Gross crude oil imports have averaged about $3.3 billion from 1975 to 1978. In 1979 they grew to $4.4 billion and this year will be between $5.5 billion and $6 billion. Our balance of payments deficit on current account has averaged $4.6 billion for the

July 8, 1980
Energy
past five years and could be in the $6 billion to $6.5 billion range this year. The cost of crude oil imports by the mid-1980s is expected to be of the order of $10 billion to $15 billion. The impact on our balance of payments is clear.
But do not let me leave the House with the impression that oil imports alone caused these payments deficits. Hon. members will recall a speech I made recently in this House when I outlined how the disastrous economic policies of the Liberal government from 1973-76-their fiscal, monetary and collective bargaining policies-brought us to this position of chronic deficits. There are signs that we are sliding back into those discredited policies. Clearly action is needed on an urgent basis to meet the challenges ahead and reduce the risks of today's unstable world. We must make no mistake; the international situation is very volatile and we are in a very exposed position.
Third World debt has grown alarmingly. The cumulative figure to the end of 1979 was some $300 billion. In 1980 this is projected to increase by $60 billion to $68 billion and by a further $70 billion to $75 billion next year. Five countries to date have been negotiating a rescheduling of debt, tantamount to a corporation declaring bankruptcy. These countries are the weak ones. Others, including the ten largest LDCs which represent two-thirds of the Third World debt, are under great stress. It is expected that other countries will be the subject of further rescheduling in 1981. it is clear that the World Bank and IMF must move to play an increasing role in this program. I urge the government to support the initiatives of these two institutions in the work they must do.
These newly industrialized countries represent promising new markets for Canada, markets where we need to improve the balance of payments deficit. But these markets may not develop because of the oil problem and we will remain exposed because of our large deficit position.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has been wringing his hands because our interest rates have been so severely affected by the U.S. government in their monetary policy. Has he ever stopped to think why this is so? It is because we are in such an exposed position through our payments deficit. Unfortunately, we are caught in a vicious international circle. As the oil price increases, it leads to further instability in international foreign exchange and money markets, particularly the U.S. dollar. Since 1973, U.S. dollar holdings by official foreign institutions have doubled from $70 billion to $140 billion, and are increasing. This overhang represents a continuing source of instability in world financial markets. So unless we take action now on a broad front, we will experience the same pattern in Canadian interest rates again.
Today the political environment in the Middle East is more unstable than at any time in recent history. Iran is totally unpredictable. This is the country which knowledgeable observers regarded as one of the most stable countries in the area only a year or so before the return of Ayatollah Khomeini.
The Soviets now occupy Afghanistan. The Soviet Union today is a net exporter of oil, about 800,000 barrels a day. In 1985 this is expected to be reversed to a net import position of
one million barrels a day, a turnaround of 1,800,000 barrels a day. The Soviets have clearly served notice that Middle East oil is not exclusively a western preserve.
This is a delicate situation, and not only from the standpoint of oil supply. A significant portion of the money on deposit in the major international banks, money that has been used to finance the balance of payments deficits of both the industrial and less developed countries, emanates from the Middle East. Any disruption in this flow of money, any disruption in this recycling process which has worked so well up to now, will have serious repercussions on, first, the LDCs and, second, the major industrial countries.
I do not want to be an alarmist, but it would be foolish for us to ignore the potential of some destabilizing element in the Middle East. At the very least, competition for Middle East oil will intensify during the same period as Canada's oil imports requirements increase, a condition brought about by the neglect of successive Liberal governments.
The rising degree of trade protection is another area of major concern, a concern which would be considerably less were we not facing a $6 billion to $6.5 billion payments deficit this year and had we not experienced a $17 billion deficit in trade of manufactured goods in 1979. Countries like Japan, Korea and Germany are facing a desperate struggle to increase exports of manufactured goods since they have few raw materials to export and such large oil and other import requirements.
In spite of the brave words of Venice, we are currently seeing national self-interest forcing these and other countries to slip into a more protectionist posture. Preferential treatment for United States produced steel by New York State, and controls on U.S. petrochemical and synthetic yarn exports to the EEC, are two such examples.
What is Canada's response? We cling to an outmoded energy policy which threatens seriously to damage our manufacturing industry. We have not learned that high energy prices and scarce supplies forced Japanese and German car makers to adjust quickly and early to the changing energy environment. Our North American car manufacturers are now in the most serious downturn in years, being badly beaten by foreign imports.
If we do not move our energy policy into this new world, other industries will follow this same path. They will also produce products geared to the energy world of five to ten years ago. Our $200 million bailout of Chrysler may only be the first of its kind if we do not move soon enough.
We must be careful not to link automatically higher oil prices to inflation. Certainly they have an impact; but the experience of Germany and Japan with inflation rates which are lower than Canada's in spite of moving to world oil prices proves that the adjustment can be made, because these are the countries which are providing the greatest competition to Canada and the U.S. For how long can Canada expect countries which have made this tough adjustment to higher oil prices to ignore the threat of our subsidized oil price in this
uly 8, 1980

eriod of growing protectionism? Surely countervailing duties n our manufacturing industries, particularly those which are nergy-intensive or use petrochemicals as a feedstock, are a far reater potential dislocation than having to adjust to a more ealistic energy policy. The longer we keep our heads in the and, the greater that threat becomes.
There is another important element in the trade picture, the urrent very damaging competition in export credits. This is an bvious result of the need to increase manufactured exports to pay for oil imports. Countries with little or no oil production have now moved to an increasing extent to subsidized manufactured exports. The Venice Summit set December 31 of this year as a deadline to agree on a new set of rules to control this damaging aspect of a trade war. To be frank, 1 do not hold out much hope for improvement in this situation. The pressures of self-interest are far too great. Canada clearly has an interest here since subsidized exports can be very costly. This represents one of the largest single items in the U.K. budget. France has been said to have embarked on a policy of financial colonization in support of its subsidized exports.
Our needs are that much more pressing because of the serious state to which we have allowed our energy and trade position to fall. But the tragic part of it all is that we in Canada had and still have some options. Japan, Germany, Korea and France have no options. They continue to import oil and fight to increase manufacturing exports. We expect at an early date to be presenting to the House of Commons some views of these options as they relate to manufacturing and trade policy.
In the meantime 1 urge the government to act and tell the truth to the Canadian people. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), when he was the federal-provincial critic in the opposition and when he was sitting on this side of the House, said in this House on October 12 of last year, and I quote:
There is only one thing that matters; to be honest with the public. That is all 1 ask of the government.
Mr. Speaker, that is all I ask of this government. We have tried to give the government and the Canadian people some understanding of the present and growing seriousness of this situation, both domestically and internationally. I hope the government will listen. I hope it will face these facts and display the necessary political will and leadership and tell the truth to Canadians. Action is necessary. Action is needed now. The future is too important to Canada, and it is too precarious.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express real appreciation to the opposition for bringing forward a motion which gives us an opportunity to boast about and to explain the policies which the Liberal government has pursued in the energy field for many years. Of course, the motion was planned as, and intended to be, a political ploy to try to condemn the Liberal government and the Liberal party for their policies. The motion was worded to say that we should be condemned for a failure to have a comprehensive program. It strikes me that it provides us with
Energy
precisely the opportunity we would like to have to prove and to show how comprehensive our policy is, and how long-standing has been our awareness of the problems of which the opposition has just spoken.
I would like, for example, to point out that in 1973 the OPEC nations began their efforts by putting on an embargo which cut off oil supplies to the western world. This began to arouse the attention of the western world to the dangerous and vulnerable position in which it was situated. We found that OPEC could raise its prices arbitrarily from $2 a barrel in 1973 to $10, and then $12 within a few months, and then to proceed arbitrarily ever since to so raise the price higher and higher that it was dizzying. That was certainly evidence to the western world of the precarious position in which we found ourselves.
Our government was conscious of the need to be energy self-sufficient and, as has been pointed out already, Canada has the lowest dependence on offshore oil of almost any nation on earth, particularly any other western power. In fact, only 15 per cent of our oil comes from offshore sources, or OPEC sources, whereas the United States imports 28 per cent. Next year the United States will be 40 per cent dependent on offshore oil. Other nations in Europe, as has been pointed out, are anywhere from 75 per cent to 98 per cent dependent on offshore oil. Canada in fact is not only not energy dependent- it is a net energy exporter-but we are also in a strong position to help other nations to see their way through, and the Canadian government has tried to help them find their own solutions.
In 1973 we found that Canada, along with other western nations, faced a critical turning point. It faced the OPEC embargo and OPEC energy price increases. From then on we knew that energy would never be cheap again. It was clear that there were profound strategic problems. We do not need to be told by the opposition about those problems today.
Strategic problems were confronting us when we were dependent upon Middle East oil. We do not have to be told that now, because already in 1973 Melvin Laird, a former secretary of defence in the United States, said this was the greatest danger to the western world since Hitler and World War II. That was said by the American secretary of defence back in 1973. We certainly have been aware of the strategic dangers which faced the western world at that time.
We also realized the economic dangers and disasters which loomed ahead. In 1974 the British publication The Economist said that our world monetary system was being set awash and that this was the greatest transfer of human wealth that has ever taken place in the history of mankind. Much wealth in a short period of time was transferred to Middle East nations which had oil, and there were prospects of ever-increasing and arbitrary price increases which would force the monetary system of the western world to be set awash. Then we were told that the western world was heading toward possible recession and, in fact, to depression. We were told of the tremendous balance of payments deficits which would come about in the west as the west spent endless amounts of money

Energy
for oil and energy but would be unable to get it back in terms of sales. That might set the whole western world into a state of chaos.
We have seen what this has done to the American economy. There has been an enormous transfer of American dollars and Eurodollars to the Middle East.
We certainly also can say that we were tipped off back in
1973	and 1974 about the danger of the loss of our independence as nations in the west. This is nothing new. In 1973 and
1974	it was quite evident-it was spoken about-that certainly some of the Middle East powers would be able to exercise both blackmail and bribery. We saw that various American civil servants were bought up. They resigned their jobs to work for certain powers which were not American. They registered as agents for foreign powers. 1 refer, for example, to the former vice-president of the United States, Spiro Agnew, a certain former American defence minister, and a certain former expert in Middle East affairs for the CIA. We saw already back in 1973 and in 1974 that there were signs that foreign powers would use their wealth both to bribe and to blackmail. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) very correctly just said that those powers were going to be able to use money and force to effect foreign policies in the world and that we are in danger. That power is a threat. The hon. member was quite right.
Let us recall the Jerusalem embassy issue. We remember how the last government faced the force of certain Arab governments which came forward and said that we had to behave in a certain way, and because of their threats we did. We changed our national policy in order to accommodate them. We can also see that there are dangers which arise from this foreign force and this foreign power to blackmail, in terms of the Arab boycott, which can threaten the individual rights of Canadians, whatever their origin or religion. Arab power and blackmail can threaten action to put one Canadian business at odds with another, to force one Canadian business not to buy and deal with another, and in fact to question the integrity and the right of certain individuals to work in Canadian companies because of their religion.
Indeed, we realize the power of OPEC oil to affect the economy, to affect our military and strategic future, and to affect our monetary system. This is not new; we have been talking about it for years.
But what is important is that in order to reply to such blackmail, to such bribery and to such dangers in the strategic situation in the world, Canada has been carrying on-I happen to know this from personal experience-not only a program to try to develop alternate sources of energy but also a comprehensive attempt to try to educate the population of Canada to the urgency of conservation of energy.
I remember, when working for a non-governmental organization, coming to the Government of Canada back in 1974 and
1975	and finding that the government was producing and printing all kinds of materials for schools, for homes, for
July 8, 1980
companies and for corporations, which we helped to distribute to citizens to inform them on how to save energy, how to use CHIP, how to insulate houses, how to cut down on the use of oil in homes and factories, and how to cut back on the over use of oil and gas in automobiles. All this was being done years ago; it is not new. This opposition has to be reminded of the publications, which are still available today, which were printed years ago on this subject to help the Canadian population know how to conserve energy. Through these very important programs. I am glad that the opposition has brought to our attention the importance of concern for energy and for energy conservation, for alternate forms of energy and the proper pricing of energy. But we can see that the Canadian government has been involved in a widespread diversification of efforts to reduce our dependence on energy, and to provide not just one answer, but several answers, in a number of directions. The very capable Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has pointed out that we have, first of all, a policy on natural gas, that we have been developing a gas pipeline, for example, throughout Canada. You will remember our pipeline debates, you will remember the discussion of the Quebec and maritime gas pipeline, and you are aware of the Alaska pipeline and of the efforts to use gas as one alternative. Another alternative is coal, another is atomic energy, another is methanol and ethanol the use of which we have been trying to encourage in terms of technology, research and development. We have also been trying to encourage the development of tar sands and the use of heavy oil, implemental oil, solar and wind energy and residual oils.
1 know, for example, that when the Conservative party was in power, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who was then the energy critic for the Liberal party, tried even at that time to meet officials in southern Ontario in what we called the energy caucus. He visited solar plants and schools which were heated by solar energy, and he encouraged the use of solar energy in southern Ontario. I remember his concern about this, and in fact just a few months ago, as a result of the R & D policy of the Liberal government, a large corporation in Brampton extended its dry cleaning plant, augmenting its facilities with solar heating. There is no question that there are many ways in which we in the government try to meet our energy needs with diverse plans, not just with only one answer to the whole subject of energy.
In closing I should like to focus upon one particular area, that is, the area of gas. I agree with the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) when he speaks about the problems being faced by the United States. Perhaps he should have been giving his speech in the House of Representatives in the United States when he spoke about the dangers that were facing the auto industry there and the whole North American auto industry, the decisions concerning which are mainly made in the United States. He was correct when he assessed the problems and the vulnerability of the United States in using oil as its one source of energy.
What the Canadian government has done through the Alaska pipeline is to try to induce the Americans to run the
July 8, 1980

pipeline from Prud'hoe Bay overland down through Alaska, across the Yukon, across northern British Columbia, down through Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan, into the United States, both east and west. The Canadian government has tried to encourage the Americans to bring their own resources, other than oil, into the western United States. This would help the U.S. to face its energy problems and not to continue to depend on offshore oil.
We would thereby also encourage the Americans, if they would accept this project, to also consider the possibility of bringing their oil from Alaska overland, to protect the environment of B.C., to protect us from the huge tankers which can smash up and thus destroy our ecology on the west coast forever. I believe the Canadian government is trying to help the United States to recognize its vulnerability to dependence upon the tanker system. If we ever had a war, God forbid, the American tanker system bringing American defence oil from northern Alaska by tanker would be extremely exposed and vulnerable. Bringing it by land would be a much safer solution for all.
The Canadian government is trying to see if we can also expand our own natural gas industry by bringing in a pre-built system, and I hope this will be possible. By bringing some Alberta gas initially to the United States, we will help to increase the awareness of the Americans of their addiction to the use of oil and gasoline and of the need to rely on natural gas more quickly.
The American energy system in the west is too dependent on gasoline and oil. By bringing natural gas from Alaska we would encourage the Americans to become more aware of the use of natural gas and the need for replacement of oil by Canadian gas in the western United States. Americans in Chicago and in the middle American states should also be made more aware of their dependence on oil and gasoline and of the importance of using Canadian natural gas instead. By the conscious policy of the Canadian government to try to bring the American government to encourage the use of natural gas from Alaska, and by building a prebuilt pipeline to get Alberta gas to the United States as a first step to getting Alaska gas going to the United States, we will be able to help the Americans recognize the possibility of using gas instead of oil as a fuel.
This gas project will also induce small Canadian gas exploration companies in Alberta to initiate programs to find more gas which can be used in the eastern part of Canada, which can be used in Quebec and the maritimes, and which can be liquefied and used as a substitute fuel for automobiles and larger vehicles. Canadians have been in the forefront in developing this technology as an alternative. Let us therefore be aware of the fact that in this one field alone the Canadian government is trying not only to provide a substitute for oil, as this resolution does not recognize, to make us more self-sufficient, but is also aiming at improving our economy.
Business of the House
By using gas instead of oil, we will be able to reduce our dependency on foreign offshore oil. We will be able to reduce our balance of payments deficit. It will mean the production of $2 billion worth of steel pipeline which will give jobs to thousands of Canadians in Regina and Hamilton producing the steel and the pipeline for the Alaska line. It will provide tens of thousands of jobs for Canadians involved in laying the pipeline and maintaining it where it is on Canadian soil. In every way this policy, just in the field of natural gas alone, is not only aimed at helping Canada become more self-sufficient and to provide Canadians with a cheaper ultimate source of energy, but it helps Americans to understand and learn of the value of depending on natural gas and it helps Americans to receive this on a safe overland route. Also it provides the United States with a more secure and less vulnerable source of energy. As Americans become more conscious of this, they too will develop new technologies in the use of this vital resource. Therefore they will be able to help their automotive industry and perhaps will be able to change over some vehicles to the use of natural gas.
This whole policy is not just selfish for Canada. In fact it is intended to meet the very criticisms just aimed at us. It is aimed to help the United States to meet and understand its own problems, and for us to co-operate to make it less dependent on strategic energy from the Middle East and their unstable governments, such as were described. I do not believe we should play political games with world problems. Indeed I believe we should co-operate. Therefore I should like to say I am glad this debate was held. It provided us on this side of the House with an opportunity to stand up and point out why our policies in each of the areas are indeed helpful not only to Canada but in fact to the entire western world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in rising to debate the motion presented on behalf of my party by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). The motion condemns the government for its lack of planning in the field of energy in a manner that would take care of the future needs of Canadians. I take particular pleasure in doing so today, because it was exactly six years ago that I was elected to this chamber, the class of 1974. I remember very clearly the campaign on which we were elected at that time, we of the class of 1974. At that time we were debating wage and price controls, and there were very hard decisions to make.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: The Grits do not remember that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
They have a lapse of memory on that score. The prime minister of the day went around saying that it was not necessary. I remember very clearly that western Canada in particular was willing to make very tough decisions to meet the future needs of Canadians. They were willing to do that, even though that concept was not naturally acceptable to us in the Conservative party. We were willing to take that short-term risk for the long-term gain and benefit of Canadians.
I heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) today talk about all the things the government was doing, as though the Liberal Government of Canada is free to do all those things. But I would remind him of an old French proverb which says, "He who drags his chains is not free". I would point out that the Liberal government has some very, very obvious chains it is dragging about which limit its activity. Therefore it is no longer free to do what it wants.
The first one is the chain of deficit financing. The Liberal government talks in grandiose terms of doing what it wants, and all the time it spends beyond its means and imprisons itself to world economic forces. That ought not to be the case if it were running its ship the way it should. The second one is the chain of lack of planning for the future of Canada. The third is the chain of having to depend on offshore sources of energy. Today we are depending on offshore sources of energy when it was just a matter of ten years ago that we were net exporters of oil. Is that planning on the part of the government? Is that being creative? "He who drags his chains is not free".
I want to remind the Liberal government that the western part of the country was willing to take a tough decision in 1974, it was willing to take it in 1980 as well. The major fault
July 8, 1980

I would assign to the Liberal government is its continuing fault of trying to suggest to Canadians that there are easy panaceas for very difficult problems, that we can spend our way into prosperity, and that no one has to pay the extra cost which energy is naturally costing today. They suggest that we do not have to pay that 18 cents or more for the extra cost of production today. They say that there are easy solutions to very difficult problems. The crime of the Liberal government is that it is doing this at the expense of our children and grandchildren. They are the ones who will have to pay the bill.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as we broke for the dinner hour I was saying that the success of the Liberal party at the polls lay in the fact that they were able to convince the majority of the Canadian people there really are easy solutions to the most difficult problems we face, whether they are in respect of the economy, wage and price controls, energy or, the 18-cent excise tax that was to be placed on gasoline. The Liberal party was able to convince the voters there was an easy solution to this most difficult problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: You don't know what it is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) loves to talk but he does not perform very well.
The crime of their success lies in the fact that in both cases, in 1974 and in 1980, they made our children and our children's children suffer for a delusion they were able to perpetrate. This is not a matter of solutions they have provided, but postponement of those solutions.
If they had been successful on the political stage at home they would have moved on an entirely different platform, particularly when they move into energy negotiations around the world. It is a different stage, it is different players and there are different stakes. On the world stage it is a matter of survival, not simply a matter of re-election.
Domestically they have been able to pull it off as far as re-election was concerned, but the great concern I am sure of Canadians is that the Liberal government, because its major concern is one of public relations rather than of substance, is going to be snookered when it comes to working with the big players on the international stage.
Energy
Incidentally, I might add, it is strange in the last week that the governments of Mexico and Venezuela have announced at least $1 per barrel increases in petroleum prices, without one whimper from the Liberal government regarding what it will cost the Canadian taxpayers for that increase in the price of petroleum products, yet let the premier of Alberta suggest that the price of Canadian petroleum ought to move to at least 50 per cent of world prices and he becomes greedy and selfish. He becomes everything but a Canadian. Somehow there is a double standard in the Liberal party on that score.
I recall watching on television just the other day the president of Dome Petroleum saying that the difference is not a difference between $34, the world price, and $ 14, the domestic price, but really a difference between $34 and $5, because the $14 per barrel domestic price means that the provincial and federal governments receive the additional $9 and the oil companies receive only $5. However, the Saudi Arabians, the Venezuelans, the Mexicans and those in Kuwait are receiving the full $34 price. Guess where those companies are going to go, those companies which are receiving only $5 on the domestic scene? If they have a choice of $5 return per barrel in Canada and $20, $30 or $35 in the United States, Mexico or Venezuela, guess where they are going to go? We are pretending that in Canada we can suppress the price of energy, keep it artificially low, and still maintain or achieve self-sufficiency in petroleum products.
On the world stage, while countries are mildly concerned about price, they are not concerned so much about price any more as they are concerned about security of supply. That is now the name of the game. It is the future and the existence of those countries about which they are worried. While members have been talking about the tragedy that Third World countries are facing because of increases in the cost of energy, the real question is, will they make it at all? One hon. member referred to this just before the dinner hour. Some of these Third World countries have effectively declared bankruptcy already. They are rewriting their loans. The name of the game in those countries is survival.
If we are to look only at price then surely we are going to lose out on security of supply. The price is important, but on the world stage the very fact that security of supply is an issue, means there is going to be greater competition for a diminishing source of supply. As the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands pointed out in her speech earlier, Russia is competing for world supply now. I do not know how many Canadians are aware of the fact that the greatest producer of petroleum in the world today is not Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Iraq or Iran, but the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union produces almost 12 million barrels of petroleum per day and is a net exporter to the satellite countries. It is also exporting natural gas to western Europe. However, this is the last year in which the U.S.S.R. will be a net exporter. Next year it will become a net importer of oil and, when that happens, hon. members can guess what will happen in the Middle East.

July 8, 1980
Energy
Is it any wonder that the government of the Soviet Union is interested in Afghanistan, Iran, and the Persian Gulf? Is it any wonder that the Middle East countries in wanting to preserve their cash flow over the next 20 years, 30 years, 40 years or 50 years, are diminishing their production? That is why these countries are the centre of interest of all the nations of the world, because supply is the issue of the day.
The issue is not simply price. Therefore it becomes critical as to how sensitive we are in handling our foreign policy. All our friends, including the United States, will be competing for that same limited source of supply. The issue which we must face is how well we can preserve our domestic economic integrity without alienating our best friends. Earlier in the evening the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) mentioned a continental energy policy with some fear. He does not have to worry because it is already here. There is no signed continental energy agreement, but there is a de facto continental energy agreement, because there is one thing which the United States and the other countries are very well aware of, and that is Canada's budgetary problems.
The other countries know that we are in debt and that we need money. They know that Mexico is in the same position. The United States, for example, knows very well that while Mexico has vast reserves of natural gas and petroleum, and is talking about limited sales to that country, it needs the cash flow to raise their standard of living. If they know about Mexico, they certainly know about Canada. They know that we are facing a $14 billion deficit this year. They know that we are $80 billion in debt.
The United States also knows that when the crunch comes, the Liberal government, having created the problem, will try to extricate itself in the easiest plausible way, and that they will sell. Who needs a written continental agreement when one is in the kind of trouble which Canada is in in terms of its fiscal arrangement? I said earlier in the evening that he who drags his chains is not free. The Liberal government has brought the Canadian economy to such a strait that we are not free any more to decide whether or not we will sell. That is why the Liberal government is so anxious to impose an excise tax on natural gas in British Columbia.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: What about hydro power?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
There is also hydro power in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba. The United States know that they can pull it off because they know that the cash flow is necessary, that the sale will go through and that the federal government will benefit from it.
This leads us to the importance of the pre-build section of the pipeline about which some hon. members spoke earlier. The question is not whether or not the pre-build section of the pipeline will be built; the question is if and when it is built, will this Liberal government ensure that the future of Canada is protected in the transaction?
Just a few weeks ago the cabinet sought more concrete assurances on this matter from the United States. Now, the congress of the United States has passed a resolution reinforcing the intention of the Americans to build the Alaska leg of that pipeline. But what if, after that pre-build section is completed in Canada and we have invested $1.2 billion in its construction and we begin to export natural gas to the U.S., the Americans decide in the ensuing five years, in 1985, that they have a better way of providing their energy, whatever the means may be? What if the Americans decide to cash in the chips? What will Canada do then?
Does this government have any kind of alternatives or contingency plans in case the Americans decide after five years that they do not want to build the Alaska section of that pipeline? What are their contingency plans? Are they, for example, willing to subsidize the pre-build section afterwards? Is there a contingency to increase Canadian sales of natural gas to the United States, because Canada needs the cash flow? Will that contingency plan be to extend the natural gas pipeline up the Mackenzie Valley to the Delta gas fields?
What are the contingency plans, if any, of this Liberal government? There are some limitations to the American proposal. The Americans cannot subsidize the Alaska leg of the pipeline with tax money. They cannot allow oil companies to invest in an equitable way in that pipeline, and they cannot allow Canadians to begin tracking of the costs through the Canadian section. There are some severe limitations.
Recognizing those limitations and the fact that all we have is an international agreement at this time-there is no ironclad agreement on finances-what assurances has the Liberal government extracted from the Americans that Canada will not be left in a greater debt position as a result of that agreement?
The Liberal government is talking about an export tax on energy, particularly natural gas and electricity to the United States. What about the consumptive products in Canada which are produced as the result of consuming energy, the byproducts of natural gas? Will the Liberal government decide that all the resins, plastics and the energy-consuming products which are made from petroleum and petroleum byproducts will be taxed? What is the limit to which the Canadian government, because of its reckless spending in the past, is willing to go in taxing energy exports?
Will the government stop at taxing energy and electricity, or will it include uranium? What about natural gas products? How far will the government go? The fact is that the industrial complex of the United States is already shifting. It is moving from the cold north where so many of the factories have become obsolete. They are rationalizing their industries and moving them further south where less energy is required and it is closer to the sources of energy. They will be closer to the Mexican pipelines and the ships and pipelines which come up the Mississippi Valley.
What implications does the fact that the industrial complex of the United States is moving further south have on Canada's marketing of petroleum and petroleum-products to that country?
uly 8, 1980

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa Centre is mumbling again, but that is about all he ever does. How far is the Liberal government willing to go to protect the future of Canada? I said at the outset that he who drags his chains is not free. Canada has been chained by indebtedness. The Liberal government has chained itself to indebtedness and, as a result, Canada no longer has the freedom of movement which we enjoyed at one time. Ten years ago Canada was a net exporter, but today we are a net importer. That is why I fully endorse the motion introduced by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that this government stands condemned for its failure to adopt an innovative energy program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume that the motion which we are discussing was introduced by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) because, as the former secretary of state for external affairs and with her knowledge and her expertise in international affairs she hoped the debate would take on some international connotation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: That is what I was hoping.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
It is unfortunate that it has not. I must say to the hon. lady, however, that if it has not she should look around at members on that side of the House for the particular reason since most of them insisted, once again, on discussing events leading up to the last election. It boggles the mind somewhat that many, many months after the election, speaker after speaker from the opposition has taken this approach. I feel sorry for the hon. member who set the right tone and raised the international complications and implications of a worldwide energy policy, and who now finds that the debate has bogged down and become a repeat performance of the issues that dominated the last election.
1 believe it was a former minister, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), who referred again to the almost immoral action of the NDP and the Liberals in "ganging up", I think is the expression he used, to defeat the government of the day last December. It is unfortunate that he has forgotten that the real defeat was not in December; the real defeat was in February, after the people of Canada had a chance to analyse the policy of the Tory government and found it discriminatory, ineffective, and hardly suited to the 1980s.
Although the government was defeated in December by the collective vote of the opposition parties, that government had an opportunity to be returned with a greater majority, if they had not been so adamant in stating that if they were returned they would introduce again precisely the same energy policy, without the slightest change.
I think that between December and February Canadians, at first glance appalled at the thought of another election so soon, concentrated on the issues. Because the December budget was, in effect, a piece of legislation through which the Tory energy
Energy
policy was enunciated, it is logical that the debates during December, January, and February centred on it. The government of the day had ample opportunity to explain its policy to the Canadian public, to explain the need for conservation, to explain the need for a policy. The people listened and found that government wanting.
The one conclusion that I came to after listening to the debates and participating in the election campaign, was not that people were particularly concerned about paying an additional 18, 20 or 30 cents for a gallon of gas; that is inevitable-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: It is?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: It is inevitable.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: All right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE COMPREHENSIVE ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
What is important is that the increase should not be imposed in the discriminatory manner in which the government of the day was prepared to impose it.
When I heard the argument that the price had to be raised in order to conserve gasoline, I knew that it would not convince the farmers in Lincoln. Whether gasoline was $2, $3 or $4 per gallon, they would have to use the same amount to earn a living, or cultivate their land. The people could not understand an energy policy that on the one hand asked them to leave their automobiles at home and use public transportation and, on the other hand, put an excise tax on transportation.
Fishermen could not understand how they were expected to cut back on the use of fuel and gasoline despite the increase that was proposed, when the only way they could survive was to pay the tax and continue using energy.
Once again, the Tory policy seemed to say, "If you can afford the increase, so be it." As usual the farmer, the cab driver, and people who had to go to work by public transit, the fisherman-the little fellow-would be expected to pay the 18cent excise tax.
It is amazing how insensitive that governent was. It failed to appreciate that the excise tax that already existed did not apply, because of rebates, to the farmer, to the commercial traveller, to the cab driver, and to people who had to use their automobile or tractor in order to earn a living. These people rose up in anger in the last election.
I think hon. members opposite would now agree that, all things being equal, it might have been a little wiser of the Conservative party, during that two-month period, to have suggested that if they were returned they would exempt those traditional groups who, because of their profession or background or way of life, had to use gasoline, and for whom it was not a luxury.
The problem is not how much gasoline costs but, rather, that policies be applied with equity, justice, compassion and understanding-that we do not penalize that segment of society which is least able to protect itself. I suppose in many ways that is the difference between our two parties, Mr. Speaker. We in this party care about people.

July 8, 198
Energy
If gasoline were to cost $2.50 or $3 per gallon it would not prevent anyone who wants to drive a Cadillac, a Mercedes or whatever, from doing so. Those people can only be attacked through rationing. An extra 18 cents per gallon for the farmer or nurseryman in Lincoln, or the fellow who has to drive 12 miles to the steel company, or people who go to work in buses which pass on the 18 cents in the form of increased cost, shows insensitivity to their position. It is obvious that the government of the day was not defeated on its energy policy; it was defeated because of that insensitivity. I am surprised that all these months later that party still has not realized that they were not defeated in December; they simply were not re-elected in February. There is a fundamental difference there, and one that they should heed.
They had the opportunity to go to the people and say, "Look at the big bad coalition of NDP and Liberals who defeated us. They did not give us a chance. We have only been in office nine or ten months and we have only had six months to study the issues in Banff or Jasper, or whatever secluded area. We were just back and the big bad opposition ganged up and threw us out." When they were thrown out they had an opportunity to explain their energy policy to the public-why they would put an 18-cent excise tax on a gallon of gas even for the farmer, the fishermen or the cab driver. In fairness to the opposition, I must say that they tried, but smug in their arrogance about their policy they went so far as to say, "We would not change a comma-not a semi-colon. If re-elected we will do exactly the same thing."
As a government they may have underestimated the opposition, but they made a more serious error in underestimating the intelligence of Canadians who recognized their energy policy as disastrous, discriminatory, and unnecessary.
I think all of us would agree that we must move to energy self-sufficiency. We must be as independent as we can from foreign sources. The motion of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands reads as follows:
That this House deplores the Liberal government's indifference to the consequences of the global oil crisis and condemns its failure to provide a comprehensive energy program that would make Canada self-sufficient in energy.
We are self-sufficient in energy, Mr. Speaker, we are one of the few countries in the world that is self-sufficient in energy. We have a surplus. At this moment we are exporting natural gas, coal, uranium, copper-you name it. We have a surplus. Where we have a shortage is in oil, a particular form of energy. speechtext:
I am very pleased to have an opportunity this evening to speak in this debate on what must be the most important topic before Parliament this session and, indeed, the most important topic facing Canadians today, that of energy. Our future is at stake. As the previous speaker from Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) indicated, we are also concerned tonight about the future of our children when speaking about Canada's energy future.
Unquestionably a great deal more attention must be paid to the question of our energy future by both government and Parliament. Listening to the speakers from the government on this issue, I am reminded of my years at university, taking courses in policy-making and planning. My professors would stress how important planning is for business, industry, cities, families and, indeed, government. They would outline the process of planning as being three simple steps. The first was the establishment of a clearly defined goal; second, to identify strategies to attain that goal; last, to implement those strategies in a satisfactory way toward that end.
1 suggest that the Liberal government has failed at step one. What is our goal in terms of our energy future in Canada, let alone what is our strategy for our energy future? We are distinguished among nations of the world as being one with no comprehensive national energy policy. Now, like never before, we are in need of one. Now, like never before, we are in need of strong leadership. It really is a political decision and a political priority requiring backbone and courage to come to grips with this very crucial issue.
The tragedy, of course, is indicated here today in the fact that this discussion on our energy future comes up during opposition day. An earlier speaker, the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) indicated that "here is a chance to explain our policies". I ask, is this leadership from a government that waits until an opposition day before this crucial issue is discussed in Parliament? Is this courage being demonstrated by the present government?
In his speech earlier today, the minister indicated that Canada has an energy policy. That will be news to many Canadians. Ask the members of his own party, what is their energy policy? Ask the members of this House what the energy policy is of Canada. Ask the oil companies. They would be happy to know. Indeed, ask Canadians what our energy policy is. I suggest that our inability here in this House to articulate our energy policy indicates the reality of the whole situation. The language we use in a sense betrays our confusion, in that tonight we are discussing a motion concerned with the lack of a comprehensive energy policy that would make Canada self-sufficient in energy.
We have read comments by various ministers and other people within the Liberal party, commenting on the need for energy self-sufficiency. We have energy self-sufficiency today in Canada. We are net exporters of energy in the form of hydroelectric power, natural gas, coal and oil. Perhaps members opposite ought to get together in their caucus and come to grips with just what in fact the wording is, regarding energy self-sufficiency.
I would like to review the dilemma facing Canada in a| particular context. Canada has the unique reputation in thel world today of being one of the most wealthy nations in termsl of its natural resources, thanks to the generosity of nature.I However, we are also the most underdeveloped industrialized! nation in the world. We devote a smaller percentage of our| gross national product to research and development than virtually all other industrialized nations, with the one exception I being Greece. We have more foreign ownership of our econo-1 my both in absolute and per capita terms than any other! nation in the world. We are the only energy-rich nation in the world that has handed its strategic oil and gas industry, and | thus its energy future, over to foreign corporations.
In an era of growing energy scarcity, we are distinguished I among peoples by using more energy per capita than any other country in the entire world. It is amazing that the rest of the world takes us even half-way seriously. The fact that Canada was even asked to participate at the Venice Summit talks can only be interpreted as a tribute to mother nature, and surely | not a recognition of leadership provided by this government. The Liberal government has failed to provide the much-needed I leadership during these crucial energy times, and there is little indication of change. Certainly we have heard nothing today | that would indicate any change for the future.
It has been seven years since the energy crisis first hit the I United States. However, we in Canada never had to face the problems that American citizens faced a few years ago- lineups at the gas pumps and serious shortages of home heating fuel. The prices being paid for gas in the United States, Europe and Japan, we have not had to face. This, of | course, has tended to reinforce and prolong wasteful industrial and consumer practices, raising energy comsumption per capita in Canada to record levels. This shows a singular lack of | leadership on the part of this government in that it has failed, and I must stress that term failed, the Canadian people. It has failed to develop actively and implement through policy the principles of conservation necessary to build a conserver society.
Surely our first line of defence in this energy battle must be conservation and substitution. The federal government has failed to promote aggressively research and development of alternative energy sources. The Canadian government has indeed supported research and promoted the development of the Candu nuclear power technology, but I suggest that the use of this technology is highly questionable on both safety and moral grounds, and it is certainly unnecessary within the Canadian context. If there exists a country in the world today which does not need to run headlong into the development of nuclear technology and nuclear energy, it is Canada. What country in the world has the energy resources at its disposal that we have? 1 suggest that we are not heeding that and in fact are running headlong at an unnecessary pace.
A responsible energy policy in our country should have as its foundation a comprehensive conservation program. It is possible, for example, to match the output of a multi-million dollar

I Beaufort Sea oil well or a multi-million dollar oil sands plant Iby simply not using oil the way we do.
| There is a very tremendous opportunity to save energy in ICanada by re-insulating and improving the design of our [homes, by improving energy designs and standards across the Icountry, using automatic thermostat adjustments, more efficient industrial practices, building lighter and more fuel-effi-Icient automobiles, discouraging the use of single passenger I automobiles, improving public transit systems in our urban [centres and developing solar, wind, wood waste, tidal and Ismail stream alternative energy sources.
| A recent study by the Canadian Energy Research Institute I indicates that an annual saving by 1985 of no less than 29 I million cubic metres of crude oil equivalent is possible if all I residential, commercial and transportation sectors were mobil-I ized to introduce and adopt conservationist alternatives. This would more than match the combined output of both Syncrude Canada and Suncor tar sands plants at Fort McMurray by the year 1985, five short years away.
; Another way of looking at these conservation measures is that the savings would potentially reduce Canada's current level of oil imports by 35 per cent, a problem which has been thoroughly discussed and examined tonight by a number of speakers. This is a devastating aspect in terms of our balance of payments, and this would be a simple and very humanistic way of dealing with that dilemma.
It is imperative now, before it is absolutely too late, that the Liberal government provide leadership in this area of alternate sources of energy and substitution of energy. Unfortunately, the leadership has not come at the federal government level up until this point.
I use as an example of this a school in my riding of Kamloops-Shuswap where the local school district took the initiative and provided the leadership to construct a prototype school which would be energy-saving, utilizing solar energy for heating purposes. In terms of its energy-saving devices this school has been successful beyond the wildest expectations of the school board and its advisers, and the solar energy component has been extremely successful. I recognize that funding for this prototype was provided by both the provincial and federal governments, but from the federal government only after a considerable amount of time literally begging for a few thousands of dollars to experiment, and that, 1 suggest, is not the kind of leadership our federal government should be providing in this area.
Something more recent which I dearly hope and pray that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) considers seriously is a proposal from Seymour Arm along Shuswap Lake in my riding. A small community of 300 dwellings and a number of small forest operations plus a few thousands of tourists in the summer now depend upon approximately 50 private generators for the creation of electrical power using one thousand barrels of oil annually. Nearby three streams exist coming off the mountain peaks, and the community wishes to harness the energy in these streams and has asked the federal government for support in its effort. The
Energy
federal government should provide this leadership. The federal government could provide research and development of small scale hydroelectric technology and provide encouragement and support for the development of this small scale energy project. This would recognize that we want to use our renewable resources. It would reduce our dependency on fossil fuels, and it would provide encouragement to Canadian manufacturing firms.
I would like to end with a modest proposal in terms of Canadianizing our energy industry. Our oil industry in Canada has a very special status. It has repeatedly and with considerable success convinced the federal government and consumers that higher prices are necessary to ensure adequate energy supplies in the future. By and large 1 suspect that Canadians agree with that. What the oil industry is really saying, however, is that this business is so risky that it cannot afford to go to the equity or bond markets or to the banks to get the necessary capital to finance its exploration in energy supply programs, so what it does is add a surcharge onto the price of oil and gas products.
The consumer provides the risk capital through a higher price in the marketplace, risk capital that the oil companies do not have to pay dividends on or interest on and never have to pay back. Of course the oil companies do not explain this to the consumer because it is not enough. They want even more. That is why the consumer as a taxpayer also provides the oil companies with all those tax breaks, investment tax credits, accelerated depreciation, depletion allowances, super deletion, and deferred taxes. Imperial Oil has now accumulated half a billion dollars in deferred taxes. Rather than worry about collecting those taxes in the future, why not have the government receive ownership equal to the amount of those deferred taxes?

This would provide Canadians with ten million Imperial Oil shares, at the present value. I suspect that we are not going to see those deferred taxes ever, ever, and I suspect that ten million shares in hand would certainly be a much more appropriate approach. Considering the earlier comments, is it any wonder why the oil companies' profits are so unconscionably high? Would small businesses across our country not welcome those same benefits which we give to the major oil companies, the seven sisters? If Canadian consumers are providing the bulk of risk capital used for exploration by the oil companies through paying higher prices at the pump, they should be receiving an equity position in the oil companies for that investment.
For example, if a person were to buy 4,000 litres of gas from Gulf Canada during the year and, out of an average price of 25 cents per litre, Gulf spends two cents on exploration, then this consumer over the year has financed $80 of Gulfs exploration package. If Gulf common stocks are selling now at $30 a share, then this consumer should be entitled to two and two thirds shares of Gulf for that particular year.
Energy
We must give large foreign oil companies credit. The Canadian government has allowed them to charge higher prices, part of which is used, by their own admission, to provide risk capital for exploration and to expand further their ownership and control of Canada's energy resources. They do not have to pay interest or dividends on this money and, what is more, they do not even have to pay it back. It would be a big step into the twentieth century for this Liberal government to recognize that it is the Canadian consumer through paying higher oil and gas prices, and the Canadian taxpayer through generous tax and investment incentives to the oil companies, who are really financing the development of Canada's energy resources. Consequently, we would go a long way in repatriating our energy resources if we required foreign-owned oil companies to provide Canadian consumers and taxpayers with equity ownership in exchange for their, so-called, investment.

I think it would be useful, Mr. Speaker, to put on the record a barn-burner of a speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made when he was campaigning in Halifax on January 25. In this hemisphere we have the potential of getting oil from other nations. We do not seem to have done too well with Mexico. I suggest part of the reason we have not, as was indicated by one of our speakers today, is that we do not have the financial muscle any more to make the kinds of deals that are advantageous with some of the oil producing nations.
One country which has been overlooked and which shares the extremity of this hemisphere with us is Argentina. Argentina is rapidly approaching energy self-sufficiency the same as we are. In its territory of Tierra del Fuego, the explorations for oil, some of which are being carried out by Canadian companies, will soon make that country self-sufficient in oil. As well, Argentina is providing a market for Bolivian natural gas to help that country, and it is thinking of entering into an arrangement with Brazil, not only with respect to natural gas but also with respect to hydro power to stabilize the energy needs of that region. It is at potential major suppliers of energy, such as Argentina and Mexico, that this government ought to be looking in order to supplement our own position until we are able to develop some of the alternate sources of energy to which many speakers have referred this evening and earlier in the debate.

Energy
We seem to have forgotten very quickly the lessons the OPEC nations tried to teach us. We continue in this country to buy expensive oil from OPEC. We do not want to pay this money to Alberta. We would rather buy it from OPEC. By keeping an artificially low price in this country, we encourage the wasteful consumption of that commodity which costs our federal treasury so much to import. Unless we do something to become more realistic in our attempts to balance the needs of this country, we may very well have to go back to some kind of rationing.
It seems to me that there is something extremely wrong when a country like ours which is selling petroleum and keeping the price artificially low domestically also is subsidizing the automobiles, aircraft and fishing fleets of other nations at the same unrealistically low price. If we are to encourage Canadians in all walks of life without restrictions whatsoever to burn precious petroleum, particularly gasoline, without charging them the proper price, then we may very well have to consider imposing some kind of allocation or rationing on people who do not need to burn this much gasoline to make a living. Right now anyone can go out and drive as much as they wish in as energy-wasteful a car as they want to purchase, without any inhibitions whatsoever. We just wonder how much longer this can go on.
Not many months ago the Prime Minister, in his widely-publicized speech in Halifax, told the Halifax Board of Trade that we must move on our oil problems now, but we must also think ahead. I would like to see some indication that he is thinking ahead and will do something. On page two of the speech he went on to say something very profound when he talked about the OPEC countries. He said:
I say that what is good for OPEC is not now in the interest of Canada.
I wonder if it ever was in the interest of Canada. We can only reflect and try to learn a bit from the lessons of history how advantageous it might have been if western nations and western oil companies were a little more forthcoming in the price they paid OPEC countries for oil ten years ago. It was only after some of the young, middle-class or upper-class people from those countries had the opportunity to come to western universities, see for themselves what the situation was and then go back to Arabic countries, that they realized how they were being cheated out of a non-renewable resource and how they were selling their resources-in many cases the only resource they had-for something over $1 a barrel, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, while enormous profits were being made and enormous wastes were being caused by the profligate use of that precious, non-renewable resource. But those days are over, and now the western nations and even the Arabic countries themselves are paying for them. This is because of the tremendous amount of inflation and international tensions that are caused and have been caused by the unwise and shortsighted use of a very precious commodity which is rapidly running out.
To be regional for a moment, as far as the needs of Atlantic Canada are concerned, it seems to me that as the development of Hibernia oil becomes more and more promising, there could

be no higher or better use of that commodity than to proceed I to carry out the project discussed about a year ago by our I government and the United States to fill some salt caverns in I the Strait of Canso area, or the abandoned mine on Bell Island I with some petroleum from Hibernia. At least then we would I have some security of supply, and from there we should I immediately try to stockpile other sources of petroleum and move into other commodities, whether they be foodstuffs or strategic metals. It does not seem logical or reasonable, taking a close look at the international scene, that the Soviet Union or indeed many other nations will continue to refrain from, if not acts of aggression, then calculated acts in their own self-interest.
We in Canada have not been nearly shrewd enough in the way we have conducted our affairs. I guess all of us in the House of Commons and all of us, period, are equally guilty in that we have not highlighted some of these concerns years ago. If we took better care of our country, if we managed our country better, we would not be in the state of tension and the state of constitutional unrest in which we are today. I only hope the government opposite are not using some of the understandable concerns of this country about the constitution to mask their own incompetence in running this country for the last number of years, which has contributed to this very unfortunate situation for us.
It may be a bit irrelevant, but 1 must put on the record my own concerns in this respect. I am far more worried about some of the well-meaning but over-enthusiastic constitutional reformers than I am about any separatism either in the east or the west. Basically I think we have a very sound country. It is unfortunate it has not been run better. Rather, if we could fine-tune our Constitution and make some revisions in it, whether it be in telecommunications, an elected Senate or what have you, instead of, to use an old German proverb, "throwing the baby out with the bath water", we would be much better off. Indeed it is refreshing to be here this evening talking about matters of energy, global energy concerns and something which is basic to the autonomy of our country, rather than trying to get through the semantics of some of the rather obtuse arguments being put forward under the guise of national emergency respecting our constitution, a constitution which has served this country pretty well ever since confederation.
