Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to take part in this debate tonight to address the motion put forward by the official opposition which may have set a record in this House by its vagueness. The motion condemns this government for its "failure to provide a comprehensive energy program for Canada." I find it a curious position to be put forward by members opposite.
uly 8, 1980

(2120)
This morning I forced myself to re-read the Speech from the hrone delivered on October 9, 1979. 1 had anticipated a party hich knew what a comprehensive program was not would now what a comprehensive energy program was, and that it ould be reflected in the Speech from the Throne delivered by he leader of that party. What I found was four statements, nd I would like to read those four statements to you, Mr. peaker.
First, it stated the way to build a whole nation is to respect ur individual parts; second, agreement in principle has been reached with certain coastal provinces concerning offshore mineral resources; third, self-sufficiency in energy by 1990, and this would be accomplished in consultation with the provinces, and seek to encourage a reduction in Canada's over-all energy consumption, and stimulate expansion in our capacity to supply and distribute energy in various forms and, finally, accept and respect provincial jurisdiction over resources.
Let me suggest that members read the Speech from the Throne delivered on April 14, 1980. The first thing you will notice is that this document reflects criticisms made by the leader of my party on October 10, 1979, in his response to the four points I have just mentioned which were put forward by the now right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
The second thing you will notice is that this document offers a ten-point energy plan based on two goals; first, achieving security of energy supply at a fair price for all Canadians and, secondly, strengthening national institutions while at the same time making them more responsive to provincial and regional goals.
On October 10, 1979, Mr. Trudeau stated:
I need not remind this House that the problem of guaranteeing a sure supply of energy to Canadians at a price they can afford is the most urgent and critical economic issue facing this Parliament.
This position has become a commitment for the Liberal government.
Speaking to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association on May 27 of this year, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), who has already spoken so admirably in this debate, stated:
Our aim is to give all Canadian consumers a fair deal... to keep the economy growing and keep the national debt within bounds; above all, to hold the country together. We need a pricing policy that serves these aims, not the policy aims of foreign and not always friendly nations.
A single national price for consumers of oil is one of the ten policy initiatives referred to in the Speech from the Throne of April 14. Others include an oil price based on Canadian conditions and circumstances; the establishment of the petroleum price auditing agency to report on oil company costs, profits, capital expenditures and levels of Canadian ownership; the maintenance and expansion of Petro-Canada; the creation of a new Canada oil and gas act for preferential rights for Petro-Canada and other Canadian companies of federal land and the establishment of new and more demanding requirements for exploration and development in frontier
Energy
areas; and 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry by 1990.
A sixth initiative is the reduction of dependence on imported oil by promoting conservation and stimulating production of new domestic energy supplies.
This final area is an area which I have followed very carefully since coming to Ottawa in 1975, especially since becoming a member of this chamber on May 22, 1979. I wish to spend the remainder of my time addressing the issues of conservation and renewable energy sources in this debate.
The energy conservation program which exists in Canada, and I repeat the word "exists" because it does exist, started to come about in a very meaningful way in 1974. It was conceived in that year when the initial OPEC crisis occurred. It was conceived and implemented by an earlier Liberal government. I will deal with conservation in terms of various sectors. There are four sectors with make sense in dealing with a conservation program. First of all there is industry; second, commercial and residential; third, transportation; and, fourth, research and development.
Hon. members who have preceded me in this debate have indicated that the previous Liberal government did nothing in the area of conservation, did nothing in the development of renewable energy resources, and did nothing in the development of alternatives to the use of oil and gas. I tell you that is pure nonsense.
In the area of industrial energy conservation the industry program is operated on a voluntary basis through 14 industrial energy conservation task forces established in 1975. Some of the measures available under this industrial energy conservation program are: first of all, assistance to undertake energy audits at the plant level so that a firm can determine how much energy it is using, where it is not using energy efficiently and what can be done to improve energy efficiency of the operation; second, co-operative government-industry communications programs which include publications, seminars and regional workshops between government agencies, academic and industrial units; a pilot project in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to provide grants for consultant advice and capital equipment to improve energy efficiency; an industrial energy conservation research and development program to encourage the development of new or modified energy efficient processes; and studies to determine the potential for co-generation in Canada, and the identification of opportunities to improve energy efficiency in various sectors of the industry.
Industry has essentially achieved its 1980 over-all goal to improve energy efficiency by 12 per cent since the program commenced in 1975. The task forces' new goal is to increase efficiency beyond the 12 per cent to 23 per cent by 1985.
In the area of commercial-residential energy conservation, there are several major thrusts in the housing area: there is the CHIP program-the Canadian Home Insulation Program; there is the home insulation program in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia which has some differences from CHIP;

July 8, 198
Energy
there was an oil furnace retrofit pilot project introduced to help individuals improve the efficiency of their oil furnaces in their homes; there were energy efficient new housing demonstrations put on by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources; and there was the Enersave program, a computerized home energy audit available free of charge to Canadians. It recommended cost effective actions for reducing energy consumption through re-insulation and thermostat setback techniques. All those measures were in the area of housing. The suggestion was that there has been no energy conservation program at all-I can see that already!
Having regard to buildings outside homes, a national federal policy has been formulated toward the development and application of building energy codes and standards to improve these for greater energy efficiency and energy conservation. In this area there has been an energy conservation task force network providing a forum for information transfer, training, research co-ordination and other activities designed to stimulate energy conservation.
I could go on and on in these areas. There is an internal program in the federal government, the "Save 10 Program" which was to improve the energy efficiency of federal government buildings by decreasing energy consumption by some 10 per cent. That program has been successful. It has saved $100 million in cost to this federal government alone since its inception.
In the area of transportation, Mr. Speaker, there have been all kinds of energy conservation programs introduced since the 1974-75 fiscal year. We have seen standards for the average fuel consumption of new automobiles, fuel consumption labelling, publications such as the "Gas Mileage Guide" and "The Car Mileage Book" and we have seen the tax on automobile air conditioners, which consume a substantial amount of fuel.
There are a number of programs, and finally there are the energy conservation R and D programs. The main priorities of the energy conservation R and D programs are energy efficient buildings, technology, efficiency in automotive engines, alternative fuel activities, energy systems studies, and energy efficient processes for industry. We have carried on a public awareness program to make the people of Canada understand that the energy problem is indeed a real problem, that something must be done, and that action must be taken by the individual because that is the way the transition will come about to reduce the consumption of energy.
Almost every household in Canada has received or been in touch with at least one of the brochures or booklets which have been put out by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, whether it be "One Hundred Ways to Save Energy and Money in the Home", "Billpayer's Guide to Furnace Servicing", the "Garbage Book", "Keeping the Heat In". All these types of information programs were initiated to give the Canadian consumer a means of understanding how they can help themselves by conserving energy. There are similar programs in industry and business.
There are newspaper programs. We have all seen the televi sion and radio advertising on energy conservation. There ar films, conservation vans and so on. There are also the van which went through Europe and which were acclaimed as on of the most advanced energy conservation information system in the world.
It is amazing that the opposition can say, "Oh well, ther has been nothing done, no energy conservation programs intro duced at all".

I suggest that she talk to the hon. member for Saskatoon Wes (Mr. Hnatyshyn). He will admit that the Department o Energy, Mines and Resources had a vast number of programs which were on line and moving ahead when he took office as minister of the department, and which are going on now. There are a great many more programs coming up.
I was fortunate enough, prior to the election of May 22, 1979, to be part of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and involved in the human behaviour aspects on research energy conservation. We were doing a vast number of research projects on how we could help individual Canadians move from an energy consumptive environment to an energy conserving environment. In fact our research program which we put together in conjunction with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of the Environment was one of the most advanced programs in the entire free world.
We were called upon by countries in Europe and the United States to enter into joint research projects because we were ahead of these countries, not behind them. We were not sitting around doing nothing about energy conservation. We were laying the groundwork for the kinds of energy conservation programs which will be implemented in the 1980s and which will make Canada a leading nation, not a trailing nation, in energy conservation in the free world.
We can talk about what the hon. members for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), and Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said with regard to price not working. All the research we did during the time I was in behavioural research in Consumer and Corporate Affairs indicates just the opposite, that in fact price does work. However, what price does not do is work overnight. The transition between a high consumptive society where there are massive investments by individuals and businesses in capital equipment which is energy consumptive, energy inefficient, takes years, years to replace and to make the transition from an energy consuming society to an energy conserving society.

We did start in 1974 those programs which are on line and which are now having their effects. They are good programs and they will be improved. The idea that nothing has been done because something did not happen overnight is absolute sheer nonsense. The fact is that it takes time and that it is happening. Price can and will change behaviour, but it does not work overnight.
Over time the difficulties which are being faced right now by, for example, Chrysler and Ford in their automobile sales, because they are selling relatively fuel inefficient automobiles, will be ironed out. People are changing their consuming habits. But it took many years for people to realize finally that in fact the energy crisis is real and that they must switch their purchase patterns from large automobiles to small automobiles. Unfortunately the automobile industry of North America did not pick up the signals which were there at the beginning. They did not change their production patterns. As a result we have seen a massive increase in the sales of Japanese cars, German cars, French cars and other foreign fuel-efficient cars in this country.
If the North American auto industry is to have any future it will have to bring in highly fuel-efficient automobiles. In fact the industry is moving in that direction at a very rapid rate. I am afraid that it waited a little too long before beginning, but it is moving in that direction. The fact is that the signs were there. Canadians and Americans were receiving the price information and energy information which was coming forth through the OPEC crises and the successive increases in oil prices. They were saying, "Something is happening. Is it real? Will it last?" And over six years, seven years, eight years the transition started. And now it is moving and industry will have to make the kinds of adjustments about which we are talking. We are now seeing that the auto industry is in the process of making those adjustments.
It takes time, but the price system works. However, I would suggest that it is not the appropriate way in which to adjust to a situation, particularly in Canada where there is relative richness in energy. It is a form of massive societal masochism to say that we must immediately go to world prices because it is good for the people, because it is somehow good for our souls if we go through a situation of biting the bullet. That term is so appropriate, but the problem is that the bullet is in the gut and they are pulling the trigger.
Price will rise because it must rise. However, in Canada where there is the unique opportunity to make an orderly, stable transition from a highly energy-consumptive society to a conserving society, because of the fortunate state in which we find ourselves, why is it absolutely necessary, as the official opposition would have us believe, that we immediately go to world price which would immediately create massive turmoil in this country, when it is not required?
The energy policy which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is putting forward is precisely designed to avoid the
Energy
kind of traumatic adjustments which would be brought about by the energy policy which was suggested by the individuals in the opposition. The reason that they are in the opposition is because they did not realize the simple fact that the people do not have to be beaten over the head before they will change their ways. They can be led in the process.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate. I felt compelled to deliver an address today on the very important resolution brought forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald).
This is an auspicious occasion for some of us. For those who were first elected on July 8, 1974, this is an anniversary of sorts. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Postmaster General (Miss Nicholson) is in the House. She is one of those who entered the House at the same time as I, and I just wanted to take the opportunity on this sixth anniversary of the election of a very good group of members to call the occasion to the attention of the House.
The resolution before the House is not only very appropriate at this time but it underscores the desperate circumstances in which we find ourselves today in Canada, due to the inability
2688

Energy
of this government to realize that not only do we require an energy policy but that we must make a comprehensive examination of the problems facing this country and the world.
This government took office some five months ago. Since then the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has attended a number of international conferences. It has been my impression, and that of many other people in Canada, that our participation in those international conferences has been minimal. Our representatives have sneaked in and out of those conferences as the proverbial Arab slips across the desert, without participation in events and without any real knowledge or understanding of the problems that face us.
1 would reiterate the point made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands in opening the debate when she pointed out that the OECD issued a report today which castigated Canada on its record of oil importation and oil conservation. It is the second worst record of all industrialized nations. That is an indication of the severity of the problem we face as a country and a participant in international dealings on the energy front.
Between 1960 and the mid 1970s world demand for oil almost tripled, while production in the United States, the world's biggest producers, began to decline in 1970. A large body of opinion believes that in 1975 the world reserves began to turn down. The world is now burning some 20 billion barrels of oil a year, and the drills are only adding in the vicinity of 11 billion to reserves. This basic truth has been masked by the fact that recession reduced oil demand, and new oil from the North Sea and Mexico cause a temporary glut. This has now been worked off. Demand now exceeds supply, perhaps by a million barrels a day; no one is quite sure. It is a good guess there is a lot of oil still in the ground. But a guess has no market value. Available oil is a dwindling resource.
In the past technology has baled us out, but our problem today has no precedent. Earlier transitions-from wood to coal, from whale oil to gas-came about because a superior fuel was attainable. This time, I regret to say, there is no bail-out in sight. Research can certainly help to develop new energy sources but, ironically, high energy costs leave less money for research.
In fact the belief that we owe our affluence to our technological breakthroughs seems, in retrospect, to be no more than a half truth. The whole truth is that abundant resources, especially cheap petroleum, made everything from mass air travel to high yield agriculture, possible. Energy-intensive machinery skimmed the cream off high grade resources and gave us the money to fill our homes with appliances and gadgets that give us the energy equivalent of 80 manservants a day. We are now putting out five to ten calories of energy to produce one calorie of food, and already we are looking back on cheap food with nostalgia. It is cheap and abundant energy, not the magic of technology, that has been the essential dynamo of progress.
Now we stand at the end of an awesome discontinuity: the beginning of the end of the petroleum era, the end of living off
July 8, 1980
capital, the end of rising expectations. We will still be using petroleum well into the twenty-first century, but even our optimists realize it will not be cheap. The price of OPEC oil in Montreal is now in the vicinity of $36 per barrel. The higher prices have slowed demand. World recession could bring a brief glut. But the Iranian cut-off revealed how narrow the margin of surplus is. Any serious shortage could bring a surge in price. What are the chances of this happening?
Prophecy, of course, is even riskier than politics. Which of our economic projections considered the Ayatollah Khomeini, or the Arab oil boycott, or the accidental break in the TransArabian pipeline? When you are looking at the mid-east supply and demand-and that is where the crunch will come, because that is where 80 per cent of the oil for export is being pumped-the incredible often looks only too much like the probable.
The main key to supply is Saudi Arabia. The Saudis have had, until recently, enough spare production capacity to hold down the world price if other producers tried pushing it too high. Between 1974 and 1978 they dropped the real price of oil by 20 to 25 per cent. Even now they have set their selling price at something like $28 or $30, well below the price asked by other producers.
The Saudis are concerned about the economies of the western nations, their chief customers and chief investment outlets, and they are afraid that a deep recession would strengthen the communist parties of Europe. As demand has risen, the Saudis have run into pressure problems in trying to raise production capacity and have in the past year reduced the level 10 per cent to their present 9.5 million barrels per day. As the financial cost of controlling OPEC rises, conservation looks even more attractive. Like some other Arab producers, they have more income than they need, and there is no economic reason to deplete their oil so quickly when later it could be worth so much more. After seeing how too fast development brought corruption and chaos to Iran, they might well want to slow their massive industrial development program.
Most OPEC producers hold similar but even stronger views, and it is anticipated on the basis of announcements now made that we can look forward to a reduction of some three million barrels per day. Right now OPEC is producing about 30 million barrels of the 51 million barrels per day the world is burning. The best we can hope for from OPEC in the late 1980s in an increase of 20 to 25 per cent.
This is not too reassuring when we contemplate future demand. The Third World is expected to grow by six or seven per cent. By 1985 this could add 40 per cent to their oil needs which are now about five million barrels per day. For example, the Mexican economy is growing so fast that by 1985 it will probably need half its estimated output of three million barrels per day. By then the OPEC countries, with their huge development programs, will likely be using another five million barrels per day themselves.
Production growth has slowed in the Soviet Union. The Soviets supply nine-tenths of the oil used by eastern European countries, and have told the eastern Europeans not to expect
July 8, 1980

these supplies to be raised. Increased western demand alone could take all of OPEC's late 1980s' production, and if we add this new demand we could possibly all be scrambling for a static supply of Middle East oil in the 1990s.
Nor can we shut our eyes to the tensions in this area. In the last three decades the Middle East has had half a dozen wars, a dozen revolutions, and innumerable assassinations. It is the heartland of terrorism, the politics of desperation, and an endless chain of tankers pass through the Straits of Hormuz carrying half of all the OPEC oil that powers western civilization. A supertanker sunk in the mouth of the straits could cut this lifeline. Significantly, Lloyds of London, the world's leading underwriters, have designated the Persian Gulf a war risk area.
Uncertainty is the order of the day and no one can predict what the price of oil will be next year, let alone in three or four months time. After the oil embargo in 1974, 20 OECD nations formed the International Energy Agency to co-ordinate a common approach to consumption, and much depends on its members meeting their year-end targets: a cutback in consumption of two million barrels a day which is about five per cent of the western world's oil demand. The less oil we use collectively, the less chance of further disruptions and the slower the world price will rise.
Notwithstanding the disregard which this government has shown with respect to its commitments internationally, Canada does have a big stake in the International Energy Agency. Any significant rise in price will intensify conflict between western allies, between the west and the communists and between factions within nations. Every 10 per cent rise in the world price adds one half a percentage point to OECD inflation. A sharp rise would strain the world monetary system and shrink world purchasing power. What price is Canadian self-sufficiency if we cannot sell our goods on the world market? We have to take our part in bringing supply and demand into balance.
Last July Canadian targets were set by the previous government. They were set by the former prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). We agreed at that time to reduce our net imports of oil by 100,000 barrels a day throughout 1980, to hold the 1985 imports to 600,000 barrels.
Recently the late Prime Minister Ohira of Japan spoke to this Parliament and he reiterated the necessity of the western industrialized nations reducing in a substantial way their imports of oil. The present government has not yet come to grips with this reality. At the last Summit there was great pressure on the Prime Minister and the delegation representing Canada to reaffirm the commitments made at the Tokyo Summit.
These targets that we have set for ourselves are not going to be easy to meet. We are pumping crude at the rate of 1.6 million barrels a day, and that is near capacity. It leaves us very little flexibility. In Canada we are burning something like 1.9 million barrels, and that calls for daily net imports of
Energy
about 300,000 barrels. The production in western Canada is in decline and the most optimistic estimate is that by 1985 we will be short by at least 600,000 barrels a day. Some estimates put the shortage at 900,000 barrels a day by 1985. In 1990, the daily shortfall will grow, and keep growing.
The fact is that this is the background in which the international negotiations and circumstances have taken place. I want to say that notwithstanding the attempt on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to hand out press releases with respect to what has happened at the Venice Summit, there was a great similarity with respect to the resolutions which were brought forward at the Venice Summit to those that were brought forward at the Tokyo Summit. I simply say that to reiterate and underline them. At Venice there was a reinforcement of the commitments made, and an attempt to bring Canada into the mainstream with respect to the western industrialized nations on the commitments that are to be made by Canada on the international scene.
The Tokyo communique is interesting and I want to refer to it to indicate the great similarity in wording in what took place then with what the release was with respect to the Venice Summit which has just concluded.
One of the statements made at the Tokyo Summit, which was reiterated again at Venice, was:
The most urgent tasks are to reduce oil consumption and to hasten the development of other energy resources.
1 suggest this statement has a familiar ring.
What were some of the commitments made at Tokyo? One of the commitments was that we pledge our countries to increase as far as possible coal use, production and trade, without damage to the environment. Does that sound familiar? And does this statement sound familiar?
We need to expand alternative sources of energy, especially those which will help to prevent further pollution, particularly increases of carbon dioxide and sulphur oxides in the atmosphere.
Without the expansion of nuclear power generating capacity in the coming decades, economic growth and higher employment will be hard to achieve.
Further on we find this statement:
We reaffirm the understanding reached at the Bonn Summit with respect to the reliable supply of nuclear fuel and minimizing the risk of nuclear proliferation.
New technologies in the field of energy are the key to the world's longer-term freedom from fuel crises.
These are very familiar statements with respect to the leaders at Venice. It is a reiteration, and yet one would believe from hearing the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy that somehow there was a new attitude taken by the leaders. It is precisely a carrying on of the position taken at Tokyo in which Canada on this occasion was out of step and out of place. Canada was not fulfilling its function on the international scene, and in not doing that it was causing itself to do a disservice to the Canadian people as well.
I was very proud and pleased that my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, did bring this resolution forward. It does give us an opportunity to point out that notwithstanding the fact that this government has been in

July 8, 1980
Energy
power almost continuously since 1963, with the assistance of the New Democratic Party, it has not as yet come forward with a comprehensive energy policy. It is still struggling with the question of pricing with the producing provinces. So I ask what are we faced with now? It is the prospect of going past July 1 with no assurance and no idea of where we are going in terms of pricing in Canada, nor do we have an indication from the federal government or the producing provinces that they are anywhere close to an agreement.
The uncertainty is causing a great deal of concern in the industry itself. It is only reasonable that unless there is some long-term agreement arrived at, the investment that is going to be required to develop our oil self-sufficiency will not be forthcoming. We are getting involved with the Prime Minister going to a conference possibly, he says, at the end of this month within six days of the conclusion of the extension period of the existing arrangement. Do members understand, particularly on the government side, what the consequences will be if there is no arrangement or agreement with respect to energy pricing in this country? Do members have any understanding? Are members quite satisfied now to rely exclusively on imports of oil with respect to generating our industry and heating our homes next winter? What are members' thoughts on the other side with respect to the activities of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy on the negotiations? In my opinion their activities have been shameful, confrontationist, and they have certainly not given any hope to us that there will be any arrangement or agreement for any reasonable period of time.
I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada look back with some affection to the Progressive Conservative government which, in a short period of time, came forward for the first time in history with a comprehensive, national energy policy benefiting all regions of this country. We had a program that was negotiated with all the provinces of this country and with all the regions of this country.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO CORRECT UNFAIRNESS-RCMP PROVISIONS
PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO CORRECT UNFAIRNESS-RCMP PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, July 3, as recorded at page 2539 of Hansard, 1 put two questions-perhaps I should say a question in two parts-to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). My questions had to do with what I regard as unfair provisions in the Public Service Superannuation Act. This is by no means the first time that 1 have drawn attention to these unfairnesses, but it is my hope that by persisting in this effort, one of these days we will get these unfair provisions corrected.
The first one about which I questioned the President of the Treasury Board last Thursday has to do with the fact that when a retired public servant dies, his widow gets a pension of only 50 per cent of what he was getting whereas, if the wife were to die first, the widower's pension would be 100 per cent.
I know that has been the practice for half a century or more, or for as long as pensions for employment have been in effect. I know that for many years it was accepted as perfectly all right. However, 1 do not think there is any place for this sort of arrangement in our society any more. If there is anything to the modern belief in equality between men and women, surely it should be practised when it comes to retirement. I suggest that it is completely and grossly unfair that the Public Service Superannuation Act has in it this provision giving, as I say, to the surviving widow a pension of only 50 per cent, whereas it would give to the surviving husband a pension of 100 per cent.
The other complaint I made when I put my question to the President of the Treasury Board last Thursday had to do with the way a pension of a widow, in this case a widow of a retired public servant, is cut off if she marries again. Here too is a practice which has been in vogue for a long time, and society tends to accept it. Society does that because it still has the
July 8, 1980

notion that somehow a woman's place in our economy depends upon her attachment to a man. This turns up in even more sinister ways in other provisions.
1 have in mind the spouse's allowance which is paid to some women between 60 and 65 but not to others, and certain other provisions, but they do not come under the Public Service Superannuation Act. I insist that if a woman, by being the wife of a public servant-and it applies to a woman who is the wife of any other kind of employee-has earned a pension which comes to her if the husband dies, that pension should not be taken away from her simply because, to put it in language which I hope people will understand, she finds another meal ticket. Surely that pension is a matter of right. Surely it is not a form of welfare. Surely it is not just income maintenance because she does not have other means of support, and, if it is a matter of right, I think it should persist.
1 recognize that when we were discussing this in developing the Canada Pension Plan and made provisions about what happens to a widow, we included in that legislation a provision such that if a widow marries again, she loses the pension while she is married, but if the second husband dies, she has the right to pick up whichever survivor's pension is the better. I remember the amusement we had in the committee when we discussed that and decided that we did not want to make it possible for a woman to marry half a dozen men and pick up one pension after another. It really was a bit of amusement because those second or third marriages do not last long enough for substantial pensions to be built up.
I am back to my basic contention that if a woman earns a pension by being a wife and mother, she is just as much entitled to that pension, as a right, as if she had earned the income in industry or as if she had earned it by investing money or what have you, and I suggest that dropping of the pension of the widow of a public servant because that widow marries again is wrong and that this should be corrected.
I suggested the other day that I hoped that any changes which are made will also be made for the widows of RCMP personnel or personnel of the armed forces, and my hope and belief are that if the government will start setting its house in order in this area, then there will be the necessary improvements in the rest of society. That is why I want a start to be made. I have been at it for a long time. I hope I do not have to keep at it just as long to win these very necessary improvements in our pension arrangements, necessary in the light of our belief today that men and women really are equal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to excuse the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Daudlin), who is unavoidably absent tonight because his family is in Ottawa. 1 will try as best I can to answer the hon. member's question and to give some satisfaction as to the possibilities.
Adjournment Debate
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) spoke on many occasions of the benefits provided for widows in retirement plans. He is aware, I am sure, as mentioned in the House last Thursday by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) when he raised the matter, that the government has already begun a general study of the survivors' benefits provided by the pension plans within the civil service. This study was instituted after the adoption of a regulation concerning the application of the Canadian Human Rights Act to the pension and life insurance plans.
Some people think that providing for survivors' benefits favours married contributors rather than single ones; that is why the amendments proposed were deferred so as not to accentuate this discrimination. However, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Human Rights Commission in its statement declared that these benefits are not discriminatory per se although it did add that some aspects of the survivors' benefits programs were incompatible with the principles of non-discrimination.
In the course of its study, the government will take into account the questions raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as well as other related matters such as the eligibility requirements for retirement benefits when a spouse remarries and the possibility of splitting up the benefits in the case of a divorce, a matter which he did not necessarily raise. This study will encompass all retirement plans within the federal civil service and will obviously require some time to be carried out. Various recommendations concerning the proposed survivors' benefits discussed in a number of studies recently made public will also be studied.
The issues raised by the hon. member deal with two qualifications on the payment of survivor benefits; one on the amount of the benefits payable, and the other being the requirement that a spouse must have become married to a public servant prior to retirement in order to qualify for benefits. Surviving spouses are entitled at present to approximately 50 per cent of the contributor's unreduced pension. Moreover, if a surviving spouse has minor children, each child receives a pension equal to 10 per cent of the contributor's benefit, so that a spouse with four minor children will receive approximately 90 per cent of the contributor's pension. I know the hon. member knows about all that.
It is quite true that representations have been made in recent years for improvements in the amounts of survivors' pensions; some suggest raising the percentage to 75 per cent, others to 100 per cent.
The second qualification under discussion is the provision in the plans that a survivor's pension is not payable to a spouse of the public servant who married after retirement, or in the case

Adjournment Debate
of a retired member of the Armed Forces or the RCMP, where the marriage took place after age 60.
